Government over nearly 6 years has seen the GDP of Taranaki grow b y nearly 50
percent. That has got a lot to do with our business -facing policies, it has got a lot to do
2 Jul 2014 General Debate 19155
with the encouragement we have given, and it has got a lot to do with the fact that this
Government sees that building infrastructure is important.
In just a number of days or a week or two coming up, we are going to be starting a
roading project in New Plymouth. Let me tell you that when people came to me and
knocked on my door, person after person, week after week, asking what was going to
happen about the Waiwhakaiho project and the bridge, I said that New Plymouth had
had a Labour Party MP for 15 years. I asked what had happened during that period of
time—absolutely nothing. They brought to me newspaper clippings that said that this
bridge is an issue  going back to 1969. Is that not amazing? Is it not unbelievable that a
Government in that period of time, which had surplus after surplus after surplus,
neglected infrastructure? Not only did it neglect infrastructure but we know there are
issues around economic growth, development, and also road safety.
This Government has been working hard and we have a region that is being rewarded
for its hard work and contribution to the New Zealand economy. That is what a lot of
people say in my region: “Here we are  producing 3.9 percent of the nation’s GDP, from
2.4 percent of the people. We work hard and we bring great benefits.” That is true. This
Government has been very, very supportive of Taranaki.
Just last week, as the Minister of Health, Tony Ryall, announc ed today, we opened
the brand-new Taranaki Base Hospital, servicing 110,000 people from the north to the
south and from the east to the west. It is a great hospital that does a great job in
supporting and bringing excellent, state-of-the-art, modern health care.
We have a new police station in New Plymouth, which the Minister of Police, Anne
Tolley, came and opened last year. It is a fantastic police station. I went there on the
open day two weekends ago, and there I was greeted at the entrance by the area
commander, as he was greeting every person. Hundreds and hundreds if not a thousand
people, maybe even more, went through that day. I asked all of the policemen and
women how it worked and whether this space worked. They said that they loved it, that
it was absolutely fantastic, and that they have a relationship with corrections. It is the
first time, I think, Minister, that that has happened here in New Zealand. They said that
this relationship with corrections is working fantastically. They have a really  great
relationship and it is working well. So what we are seeing is excellent men and women
who are protecting our community and enabling people, as they go through the
corrections system, to come back into our city and find employment and a place where
they can be reintegrated.
New Plymouth and Taranaki are doing very well. I am very pleased to stand here
after being the local MP for 6 years and say that we continue to have good news in our
region. I am sure that my colleague the Hon Chester Borrows will  talk about what is
happening down in his part of this fantastic province.
One of the great announcements we had last weekend was about the work being done
on Mount Messenger and the Awakino corridor —the gorge there. Some people say that
what we should ha ve is a tunnel straight through that area. I asked a colleague of mine,
a friend who does tunnelling, and they said that that would be the biggest roading
project in the country—

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call and speak in this
general debate and endorse the comments that have been made by my colleagues around
the importance of investing in our future —we focused a little bit with our education
spokesperson on some of those issues today—which, I think, are in stark contrast with
the comments made by Government members, who have spoken primarily on issues
around roading projects. Look, no one is going to argue that ensuring that our regions
have decent infrastructure is import ant, but the Government is basically replacing what
19156 General Debate 2 Jul 2014
it stripped away and basically replacing what it has taken away from some of those
regional areas.
I want to reflect a little bit on the other form of investment that we need for our
future, and that is investing in our past.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Eh?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Oh, we seem to have forgotten that arts, culture, and heritage
is part of our policy area that I cover as well —children, prisons, corrections, arts,
culture, and  heritage. Heritage has become one of those issues that, for the region of
Canterbury, has, unfortunately, been sidelined in recent times. Obviously, there have
been a number of competing priorities for that region, the first of which has been —
rightly so —housing. But we have needed the Government during that period to
multitask in order to ensure that we have the retention of an integral part of
Canterbury’s tourism, their sense of place, and one of the things that has drawn so many
to that city, which has been the gothic revival style of architecture that exists in that
place. We know that there are economic gains to revitalisation of our heritage areas. In
fact, an expert on the economics of historic preservation from the United States came
out to New Zeal and not long ago and talked about the fact that for some of their main
street programmes, for every $1 of investment they leveraged $18. So there is a spin -off
to that kind of investment.
We have seen really good examples —the restoration of the old Govern ment
building, the Heritage Hotel. That is a category 1 building. The private owner worked
collaboratively to ensure the restoration of that fantastic space. Contrast that with the
loss of the beautiful Majestic Theatre building in Christchurch, which, as far as I can
tell, was removed not primarily for safety reasons. It was demolished under section 38
of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act because the Government had transport
plans that meant a widening of the road and meant that that beautiful piece o f
infrastructure was removed.
I think it is time that we listened to what was said in the Heritage Quarterly recently,
where it said: “Naturally, safety must be the primary concern but we are at a point
where the remaining buildings are not considered a s ignificant risk, or can be brought
up to standard.” We have lost 47 percent of heritage buildings in the Christchurch
central business district.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: That’s because we had an earthquake.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: We are 3 year s on and no longer are these buildings being
removed solely because—these are not buildings that fell down in the earthquake. Many
of them are ones that are being demolished under the extraordinary powers that were
granted to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority at that time, but it is time that
we reconsidered the way that we deal with heritage in that city. It is time that we
reconsidered those war -time powers. It is time that we actually had a plan for the
heritage infrastructure of that region. Labour is focused on a revitalisation plan for
Canterbury. We have talked about housing and we have talked about transport.
Tomorrow morning we will be talking about our thoughts on heritage for that city, and
how we can invest in the past in order to preserve something beautiful for our future.
Heritage is not the domain of simply the last generation. Heritage is something that
we need to keep focused on for the next generation so that we can build our sense of
identity, of place, whether it be in Canterb ury, whether it be in our small provincial
regions, or whether it be in my city, Auckland, which has decimated so much of its
historical features. Tomorrow Labour looks forward to building a plan for heritage and
preservation in Christchurch and looks forw ard to showing our positive vision for that
region.
2 Jul 2014 General Debate 19157

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I too get to my feet to say that
it is good news in the regions. I know that those people on the other side of the House
may not be all that happy about it, but in South Taranaki we had some real good news
on the weekend around the realignment of the Norm anby Overbridge. That is a big
thing for us. I know that people in South Taranaki are pretty good at political
memorials. Not too many years ago when a certain Minister of Education closed a
number of schools around Taranaki, a big sign appeared on the sid e of the road that said
“Open season on Mallards”. After last week’s announcements about the realignment of
the Normanby Bridge, it would not surprise me at all if some big round bales were got
together and a huge effigy of Gerry Brownlee was built beside the Normanby
Overbridge.
The Normanby Overbridge has been a death trap in South Taranaki for 20 years. It
has claimed 21 lives over 20 years, it has been a blight on our landscape and on State
Highway 3, and all that has been done over a number of years is to move the speed limit
and put a few signs around it. It has never ever been good enough. Just a few years ago
land was bought alongside the railway line so that the road could be reconfigured to
take away the need to travel over this overbridge. There were three bridges constructed
in the 1920s. They were all identical. One of them has been completely realigned but
the other two continue to be traps for motorists. We had the land, we had the plans, but
we did not have the dough. A series of incidents ar ound the country had detracted from
the Government’s ability to be able to construct this bridge —such as the earthquakes,
such as Pike River, such as the collapse of South Canterbury Finance, etc. —and meant
that these projects had to be prioritised.
I was absolutely ecstatic to find out on the weekend that that bridge is going to be
started next year. It is done at a time when, as the previous speaker, Jonathan Young,
said, there are other road projects happening in Taranaki that have been given the same
priority—albeit in South Taranaki we think that road safety is a little bit more important
than a bottleneck. It is good to see that it has happened.
The word from the other side is that that is an election bribe. Apparently it is an
election bribe when yo u find some money to do away with a death trap. Well, if ever I
saw an election bribe, it was coming up to the 1999 election.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Oh, what happened?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: What happened then, Mr Auchinv ole, was that the
then would-be Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition at the time—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Who was that then?

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: —Helen Clark —flew by chopper to a little place
called Ruatītī with the then would -be Associate Minister of Transport, Harry
Duynhoven, and stood on another bridge. They stood on another bridge, and that was a
bridge that superseded one that had collapsed. There was a death on that bridge. It is
known because a beekeeper f ell through that bridge and was killed. We know that the
farmer was a man called Berryman. The Leader of the Opposition at that time, a couple
of months before the election, pledged that post -election, should Labour be in
Government, Labour would then nego tiate with Mr Berryman around costs —the costs
that he had incurred having been charged before the court, having had his home burnt
down and emergency services being unable to get there and the losses that he had
incurred. Labour made big promises prior to the election and yet in 9 years in
Government it did nothing. It made one offer that was to be negotiated, but it refused to
negotiate, having stood in the election campaign and said that the Government should
be negotiating with Mr and Mrs Berryman to put  this right. In 9 years the Labour
Government did not. I am pleased to say that one of my first accomplishments as the
member for Whanganui was to go to Cabinet and ask it whether it would sort out this
19158 General Debate 2 Jul 2014
issue, and it did. So to have the other side of the H ouse talk about election bribes last
weekend, when that is their history, is huge.

items.speaker: Another good point to make is this
items.text: we know that the flea on the tail of the dog in the
next Government, if Labour was ever that next Government, would be the Greens. What
we know about the Greens is that they hate roads. They do not want to build any roads.
This Normanby Overbridge would never be built if a Labour Government ever got
elected, and that is the message for the people of the Whanganui electorate.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: We have just heard the National
backbenchers prattling on about roading projects. They never mentioned the $100,000
that they have just finished spending on a bridge  that they have renovated, which they
are now going to pull down and replace with another bridge. I think that shows
something about the fiscal responsibility of the National Government.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Just shows how little you understand about the process.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: But I say to the Minister of Police that, instead of listening to her
pork barrel politicking about her own electorate, I want to come to a topic that is
intimately involved with her portfolio of policing.
In the last couple of months in the Auckland region that I represent, we have had a
number of tragic murders, including the killing of two members of our ethnic
communities. Blessie Gotingco was murdered after being abducted on the way home
from work, walking from the bus stop to her family home. [ Interruption] Well, the
Minister can laugh about it and put it down. I happen to think that that is a tragedy for
that family, as indeed is the other case of Arun Kumar, a Henderson dairy owner who
was stabbed in the neck and murdered in front of his wife in his dairy just a fortnight
ago.
Members of the ethnic community have come to me in the last couple of weeks
because they say that they are at the front line of criminal offending in New Zealand.
They are the people who drive the taxis, they are the people who staff the shops such as
our dairies around the clock, and they tell me very clearly that their concern is about the
complacency of the Government in terms of their right to feel safe in their communiti es
and on the streets. They say that when they go to a National Party member of
Parliament, they get told the one thing: “Oh, crime’s coming down.” Well, I am sorry,
but, you know, when your husband or your father or your son has been murdered, to
have the Government say: “It’s all right, crime is coming down.” really does not wash.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: No MP has said that to them.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Actually, Minist er, I looked up your own figures from April of
this year. There were 360,000 reported criminal offences —360,000 reported criminal
offences—in the last year. And what has that Minister done about it? I will tell you what
she has done. In every Budget since National was elected, the real spending on policing
has declined.
I went to the Parliamentary Library. I wanted an independent analysis of what has
happened to expenditure on policing. Do you know what it told me? It said that since
2009, spending has bee n cut in real terms by $114 million. That is $114 million less to
spend on policing and on keeping people safe. In the last year it was down $42
million—$42 million. No wonder Inspector Greg O’Connor says publicly that this year
policing at the front line will become harder for our men and women in blue. That is
what Greg O’Connor said.
I asked that Minister in the Law and Order Committee: “Have you cut the number of
police in the last 2 years?”. “No.”, she said, and then I got this letter. It is a written
answer to the same question from the same Minister. Do you know what has happened
in the last 2 years, Minister? You have cut the number of sworn, deployed constables by
2 Jul 2014 General Debate 19159
80—80 fewer policemen and policewomen are on the street now than there were 2 years
ago.
Then I asked a question about community policing stations, because in Henderson
they say: “You know, with these kids who are out of control and have been causing
problems for months, if not years, what we really need is a community police station.”
What is the National Government doing about community policing? It has cut it by 16
stations in the last 2 years —three in Manukau East in the last year alone. It has cut St
Lukes, Blockhouse Bay. It has cut Mount Albert. That does not even include stations
like mine in Mount Roskill, which has been temporarily closed, for how long? For 2
years it has had a sign on the door of the station saying: “Temporarily closed to the
public.”, because those members do not have the guts to front up and say—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —“Actually, we’ve closed the station.” That is the dishonesty of
it, Mr Speaker. They have cut spending on policing in real terms. They have cut
spending on the police in terms of percentage of Government expe nditure. They have
cut spending on the police in terms of a percentage of GDP. They talk tough about law
and order. Their trouble is that they do not walk the talk. That Minister’s administration
of her portfolio is, frankly, a disgrace.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. As the last speaker in this
debate, I stand to support my colleagues on the outstanding work that this National -led
Government continues to do for this country when it com es to economic growth. When
we came into Government, the cupboards were bare. Actually, they were more than
bare; we found bills that needed paying. [ Interruption] Yes, in 2008 the previous
Government had left office and left a growing debt behind it —shame on you—in a so-
called time of surpluses for this country. So how did the previous Government stuff up
so badly? I know: it did not have a plan and that party still does not have a plan today.
In addition to this, there was the global financial crisis, the Christchurch earthquakes,
and the Pike River mine tragedy, followed by the Rena and, recently, the Christchurch
floods. Yet through all of this, it was this National -led Government that has remained
resolute in its mission to do the things that matter mo st to New Zealanders as we
continue to build a brighter future for everyone. It is a mission that this National -led
Government set in 2008 and one that has been recently swiped by the Opposition
because it has nothing left in its tank.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Ha!

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Yes. It is a mission that has seen the emergence of a growing
economy, planned by a carefully crafted financial plan—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: We’ve got a few more ideas than roads.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: —listen, listen —underpinned by a strong Business Growth
Agenda, an agenda for New Zealand to build a more productive and competitive
economy.
So where has this economic growth come from? It has come from the regions —the
regions, of course—and our aim is for all the regions to achieve their potential. Most
have experienced strong growth and most have lower unemployment rates. Just look at
the South Island. Unemployment is at 3.9 percent. That is low. But that is not the only
thing we are doing. We are getting our regions moving through our roads of national
significance and the regional roading projects. That is a total investment of $600
million. This will help the regions to lift production, and transport through these regions
will be made much safer with our Safer Journeys strategy.
But this is not the only thing we are doing. We have got ultra -fast and rural
broadband, which allows the faster and more efficient digital and electronic
communication, so the isolation issues faced by those in the rural sector have been
19160 General Debate 2 Jul 2014
minimised. This Government is encouraging oil and gas exploration, and we are doing
this with our environment in mind. Taranaki is a great example of such a region, which
we have just heard about before from the membe r from Taranaki. It has benefited from
oil and gas exploration —40 percent of its GDP comes from oil and gas exploration.
There are not many Taranaki people whom I have met who are sad about the region’s
economic growth from oil and gas. Just imagine the po tential benefits for the Otago and
West Coast regions.
The Government’s Youth Guarantee and increased apprenticeships plan see more
opportunities for our rangatahi to work in the many trades areas where employment
abounds. Just look at the opportunities i n building and construction in Canterbury. We
are rebuilding Christchurch in all ways, from the central city development plan to the
social housing accord. Christchurch stands on the precipice of great things as the
opportunities it presents in growing the  Canterbury regional economy go without
saying.
But let us not forget one of our key regional economic growth areas: tourism. We
have combined this with fitness and well -being in our national cycle trails. Not only do
we get fit but we get to see places t hat we would not have been able to see in a car or a
bus. We get to smell regional economic growth, people, in the rural sector, in our native
forests, and in the grand expanse of Central Otago, but the best part about this is that
everyone wins. Our gains in regional economic growth will be lost if the policies of the
left are allowed to get in there. Introducing a carbon price five times the world price and
having a capital gains tax on every productive business and farm would go a significant
way towards stopping economic growth.
This National -led Government is working for all New Zealanders. Our economy
grew by 3.8 percent in the year ended March —the third -highest in the world’s
developed economies. Growth is forecast to be 4 percent. We have a plan, we  have a
hard-working and diverse team, and we have the most outstanding leader in our Prime
Minister, the Rt Hon John Key, a leader with international respect from our global
leaders. He is the man of the people—the only man to lead this country into the future.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
In Committee
Debate resumed from 1 July on the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I can advise the Committee that the two
votes that were unavailable for consideration yesterday —Vote State Services and Vote
Sport and Recreation —are now available. They will be considered in the order of
seniority of the responsible Minister.
Vote Social Development (continued)
Vote agreed to.
Vote Defence

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: At the commencement of this debate you made
the observation, for the edification of the Committee, that votes would be debated in
descending order, according to the rank of the Minister. It is rather telling —rather
revealing, one could say—that Vote Defence is languishing way down the order, at No.
10. It is not even on the front bench. In a bygone era, not so very long ago in actual fact,
only about 30 years ago —hardly a previous geological age, by any reckoning —defence
was regarded as a matter of great importance. Ministers of Defence were regarded as
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19161
senior Cabinet Ministers. This very serious and important portfolio was entrusted to a
Minister of experience and standing—a Minister ranked no lower perhaps than fourth or
fifth in the Government. But this is no longer the case. It is not a reflection on the
importance of defence; it is a reflection on the fact that this Government appears unable
to understand that importance.
That lack of understanding is illustrated clearly by the wholly inadequate level of
funding allocated to defence by this administration. The Government trumpets the quite
mythical $500 million that it claims is additional funding afforded to d efence in the
Budget. The reality, of course, is that it is $500 million over 4 years and it will go only
part of the way to replacing the roughly equivalent amount that it has pruned out of
defence over the past 2 years. It is sleight of hand —give with on e hand and take with
the other. Two percent —that is the level of expenditure that New Zealand First would
like to see allocated to defence—2 percent of GDP. It is not a massive slice of the pie —
2 percent to ensure our sovereignty, 2 percent to secure our b orders, 2 percent to protect
our exclusive economic zone and our fisheries resource, to contribute to the security of
the region, and to support the efforts of our regional partners and allies. Two percent is
the figure Australia is working towards, and Si ngapore has already long since exceeded
it. But not New Zealand; no.
Under this Government, the defence expense is less than 1 percent, and from that
paltry sum the Government claws back revenues in the form of GST, road -user charges,
and a capital charge  that relates to the cost of servicing expenditure on major projects
and acquisitions, and then of course depreciation. The actual amount of funding the
New Zealand Defence Force has to work with is even more miserable. The defence of
the nation is the fir st responsibility of Government, and less than $1 in $100 is
manifestly insufficient as a measure of the importance of this truth.
Then what the Government spends money on, what it does allow defence to actually
procure and operate, fails to reflect the realities of the world we live in. There was never
any such thing as the benign strategic environment. In the real world there are still wars
and conflicts. In the real world nations are not always nice to one another, despite the
existence of the United Na tions. Diplomacy is a wonderful thing, but only a fool would
presume that people and nations could rely on it alone. There are times when it is also
necessary to wave the big stick.
As we debate, the Middle East is dissolving into chaos yet again. Iraq an d Syria are
embroiled in civil conflict. Russia and Ukraine are facing off. The South China Sea has
several potential conflicts threatening to spark up at any moment. North Korea is testing
new missiles. Japan is talking openly about arming herself with nuclear weapons.
In the midst of this mêlée New Zealand stands blissfully unconcerned. We have no
force in the air force, notwithstanding that it is possible to drop a Mark 82 bomb on the
beach at Kaipara, from an Orion, retrofitted with a bolt –on hardpoint. Hallelujah! The
Orions can drop bombs. They cannot jink or dogfight or avoid air-to-air missiles, defend
themselves from ship -launched anti -aircraft missiles, or even hunt submarines any
more, like they were originally bought to do, but they can drop old  20th century free-fall
iron bombs. We are safe —not! Are the air force Orions also going to be fitted with
infrared search and track, or data links, or Paveway designators so they can drop smart
bombs as well, I ask the Minister? Or are we relying once aga in, as has been the policy
of this Government, and the one before it, I might add, on the hope that we will not ever
have to use any of these things in anger.
I ask the Minister, but the reality is he probably does not know what any of those
things are. D efence is a side interest for this Minister, at best. His real passions are
finance and foreign affairs. Those things are admirable and necessary —granted. But it
would be nice, at the very least, to have a Minister of Defence who cared enough about
19162 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
defence to argue in Cabinet for a credible -sized slice of the pie. On the subject of
admirals, the navy is down to one frigate because the other one is tied up in Canada,
having an extended refit. It will be out of service for more than a year, for the duration
of which New Zealand will have one ship to patrol a maritime territory covering one -
sixth of the Pacific Ocean.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: And they can’t crew the inshore patrol vessels.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Quite right, Mr Goff. There is o ne ship. The refits to Te
Kaha and Te Mana will amount to around half the cost of replacing them. I ask why this
maintenance is not being done in Whangarei. Why is this Government not trying to get
more bang for our defence buck by growing the ability of d omestic engineering to take
on such tasks? We could be building patrol ships here. We could be, and we should be,
investing in developing a shipbuilding industry here in New Zealand, anchored on the
requirements of the military, and from there, being able to construct everything, from
coastal freighters to fishing boats. Instead, we have a navy cobbled together from
imported civilian -standard vessels, based on designs for ferries and coastguard boats,
and the like. The two poor, tired, and old MEKO 200 German frigates are being flogged
to death because they are two ships being required to do the work of four.
In the 1950s and 1960s New Zealand maintained an operational fleet of six frigates.
It was a core capability, and for a nation of 2 million people, wi th no exclusive
economic zone, it was entirely affordable. What has changed? What has changed about
the reality of the world we live in, since those days, apart from the fact that it has
become less stable and less safe? Our population has doubled, and we have a vastly
larger chunk of ocean to look after. We could be forgiven for thinking that the navy’s
tasking requirement now calls for something closer to eight frigates than two, but that
reality does not appear to have worked its way through the collecti ve skulls of this
Government, which disregards the need for credible defence, relegates it to 10 th on the
Cabinet priority list, and bases its decisions on financial considerations that have
nothing to do with defending the nation and everything to do with  making bottom lines
look good.
We have no combat aircraft, nowhere near enough of a blue-water navy, and an ever-
shrinking army that is perilously close to not being able to properly support the SAS, let
alone mount an operation on the scale of Timor, wh ere we sustained a battalion on
rotation for more than a year. The New Zealand Defence Force simply does not have a
sharp end any more, and because of that—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! We are on Vote Defence, n ot Vote
Defence Force. There are two separate votes here. The member is straying into Vote
Defence Force. I just bring him back. This is about defence, not the defence force.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Because of that, it is becoming increasingly d ifficult to
recruit and retain enough good people to maintain core capabilities. Simply throwing
money in the wrong directions within the context of an ever -decreasing budget is not
the way to approach defence. We need to address the very real issue of pay  and
conditions and acknowledge that our people are underpaid in relative terms.
But money alone will not fix this problem. At the heart of it there is a lack of
understanding of what motivates people to join the military. They do not join for
money. George Orwell said: “We sleep safe in our beds because rough men stand ready
in the night to visit violence on those who would do us harm.” That is why they join.
Good men and women join up because they are motivated by a desire to fight the good
fight. They a re motivated to fight the righteous fight, to protect the innocent, and to
stand in defence of the nation. To do that they need a military that is the sharp end, that
is resourced, and that is intended to operate as a credible force, but this Government ju st
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19163
does not get that. That is why Vote Defence is so pitifully insufficient and meagre, and
why defence expenditure is so woefully misdirected.
New Zealand First in a position of influence over Government will set this matter to
rights. We will resource defence properly and we will give it back the focus and breadth
of tools that it needs. This is a dreadful Appropriation Bill and the election cannot come
soon enough. Thank you.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Defence Force

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Eight months ago the Cabinet external
relations and defence committee produced this minute that I have got in my hands. It
had been kept secret and confidential until such time as the Government was forced to
reveal it under the Official Information Act. Why was it kept secret? Because it reveals
this point: “New Zealand now has the smallest number of personnel deployed to
international peacekeeping operations in almost 20 years.” The number of Ne w Zealand
men and women, who are superb peacekeepers, whom we have deployed today is 77 —
just 77.
When I was the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Minister of Defence it
numbered up to 800 and was generally in the 300 to 500 range. This minute,  in its last
point, urges the Government to take an active approach to considering contributions to
international peace support operations. Why? Firstly, it is the right thing to do for New
Zealand as a good international citizen. But also, New Zealand is putting itself up to be
a candidate for the United Nations Security Council, and what do we say about our
good international citizenship —that the best we can mount to help international
peacekeeping operations is 77?
I wondered about this. because I know that the Government from this minute wanted
to have more people out in the field. So why did it not? Well, the answer was given in
the estimates questionnaire where I asked the question about deploying overseas. And
do you know what the Minister of Defence  tells me? He says there is a risk that you
could not deploy New Zealand service personnel overseas in a peacekeeping operation
for more than 12 months. For 9 years we had 400 to 500 people deployed on these sorts
of peace missions, Minister, and you have run down the Defence Force to the point that
we cannot have our very good peacekeepers deployed for more than 1 year. That is a
disgrace.
One reason —and this comes out of the Auditor -General’s comments on the
Minister’s handling of his portfolio —is that b etween 2009 and 2013 the number of
Regular Force personnel has been slashed by 1,200. That is a 15 percent reduction in
our Defence Force personnel. But it is worse than that. It is worse than that, because
when that Minister did what the Auditor -General accused him of doing —breaking the
social contract with the Defence Force personnel—we reached 24 percent attrition in the
Defence Force. It was 24 percent in vital trades and in vital ranks, and it takes years, 7
to 8 years, to replace people with the skills of those who walked away from the Defence
Force.
That is why our Defence Force cannot mount a decent peacekeeping operation —
because that Minister, by destroying the morale of the Defence Force in 2011 -12, and
by cutting the Defence Force budget for pers onnel, has reduced it to the point that it
cannot deploy for more than 1 year.
But it is not simply that. There has been botch -up after botch-up. When the Minister
of Defence gets to his feet I want him to comment on why the army court martialled a
brave Special Air Service soldier, who had served in Bosnia and served three times in
Afghanistan, for stealing army equipment when they could not find any equipment
19164 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
missing. They could not find any equipment missing and that has just been
overturned—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. That matter is
still before the courts and it is best not to refer to it.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: No, it is not.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: It is.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Speaking to the point of order.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I will hear the Hon Phil Goff.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I was passed the Military Court of Appeal decision from the
court by a party to the court because the suppression order has been lifted. It is in the
public arena, however much the Minister might try to suppress it.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I will need to seek some guidance on this. I
do not have the answer and I will ask for some guidance from the Clerk. [ Interruption]
No, I need to seek some guidance on this matter. I am informed that three of the four
charges were dropped, but there is still one that has not been, so on tha t basis I would
ask the member to move on, on the Defence Force, and we will leave that matter as it is.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Speaking to the point of order, the fourth charge was not
appealed by the soldier concerned, though the military court of appeal said that the army
should consider withdrawing it. But this matter is not live before the court. It is not
under a suppression order.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: OK. Well, look, just give me one moment
while I just make sure that I have got my advice correct. All right, I have some advice
and the advice is that we can continue in the same vein.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Well, I would like the Minister to explain to the Committee why
the army court martialle d a solider for the theft of equipment that was not missing. The
Minister will know that that soldier spent $15,000 of his own money on buying
equipment. It may well be that he passed back his own equipment and sold equipment
that was the army equipment, b ut there was no intent of theft, and the military court of
appeal damned the judgment that had been made in the first instance.
Do we have so many brave and experienced SAS soldiers that we can court martial
them, effectively humiliate them, and drum them  out of the military, only to find that
the military court in the first instance got it wrong? That was a botch-up.

items.speaker: The second botch -up
items.text: why is it that people working full -time for the air force at
Whenuapai can set up a private company and tender for the  equipment that they are
working full-time on? And why is it that that matter is before the Auditor-General? That
is another scandal waiting. The third thing is Babcock. Why did Babcock, in its key
performance indicators, hit the lowest level, five out of five, which is designated
unacceptable, for 6 months? Why is it that the Defence Force is doing so badly that it is
having these problems?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Looking to what we
have just heard from both the New Zealand First member Richard Prosser and Phil
Goff, you would not believe that there has actually been so much great progress in the
Defence Force. We are talking about the Appropriati on (2014/15 Estimates) Bill here:
$535 million over the next 4 years going into Vote Defence Force.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: It is $535 million. That is something to really
celebrate, quite frankly.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: That’s less than I spent on the NH90s, for God’s sake.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I am very disappointed with Phil Goff, because
no matter how nice I am to him, I cannot get him to take a bipartisan approach and
support our serving men and women. It is very, very sad.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19165
Look, what I can say to him is that he really has been misleading —I would like to
say—there around the PKO, the peacekeeping operations paper. He knows that the
reason we h ave got relatively few people out on deployment at the moment is that we
have people who have come back from Afghanistan, from East Timor, and from the
Solomon Islands. The situation is very different from when he was the Minister. On 8
September 2008 there was a headline in the New Zealand Herald relating to Phil Goff’s
tenure as Minister, which said: “Can’t fight, can’t sail, can’t fly”. We have had to turn
that round.
What we had in 2010 was the first defence white paper in 13 years. What that did
was set the policy for defence. We said: “Look, it’s fiscally pretty constrained times.
We’ve got to be very clear about what we need the Defence Force to do. Primarily, it
obviously has to maintain the integrity of New Zealand’s borders and be able to operate
in our exclusive economic zone. It has to be able to deploy into the south-west Pacific in
cases where there may be security emergencies or where there may be humanitarian
assistance and disaster relief issues they have to deal with, and it has to be able to make
a contribution further afield.” So the policy was set, but what we knew was that there
was a funding gap there. We knew what capabilities were needed to deliver on that
policy and we followed it up with the release of a capability plan, which we ha ve just
refreshed recently, and released just 2 weeks ago. But we had this hole of well over half
a billion dollars, which was going to roll up into the 2020s to a massive deficit of
money needed to fund the sort of capital equipment that the Defence Force needs.
So we went away and the officials from the Ministry of Defence and the New
Zealand Defence Force did an excellent job at looking at all the capabilities that the
Defence Force has—about 220 of them. They costed them all. They arranged them into
11 capability sets, to deliver on the policy. At the end of that we had a very clear view
of what capabilities were needed for the Defence Force to actually deliver the effects
that the Government needs it to. We went to Cabinet and said: “Look, this is the policy,
this is the strategy, this is the capability we need and now we need this funding.” As a
result of that, in this Budget we have got this over half a billion dollars’ worth over 4
years. That is something that Phil Goff really should be celebrating.  He is being
disingenuous to say that we cannot deploy a defence force on a continuous rotation. We
can; we can do two at once, just like he could when he was Minister. The same
problems that have been there around, you know, critical trades sustaining the se
deployments, have always been there. They were there when Phil Goff was there. The
key point is that we are able to sustain these deployments.
As for the New Zealand First member, he wants eight frigates for the navy. What he
did not mention was that i t was actually his leader, Winston Peters, who cancelled the
third frigate. I know he would be very eager to go and attack any country ending in
“stan”, but, actually, that is not realistic in the current world. So when you look at it, we
have got a situation where we had no new money in defence for many, many years. We
had to make the best of what we had at the time. We redeployed resources from the
back of the office to the front.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Who paid for the NH90s?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEM AN
items.text: Ah! Phil Goff has mentioned the NH90s —
$770 million. He has forgotten, though, that you do not just buy the helicopter; you
need to be able to afford to run it and you need to have people to go in it. Phil Goff
ignored that completely. He has now left us to carry the slack.
He talks about morale and attrition. Attrition in the Defence Force is now lower than
when he was Minister. It is now 11.6 percent. Morale is now at 85 percent. So 85
percent of personnel in the New Zealand Defence Force rate their morale as good or
better. I can tell you that that is a damned sight higher than the Labour caucus’ morale.
19166 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: No, no, no, not true—satisfactory.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Yes, i t absolutely is. That is 85 percent. So,
actually, what we have done is turned round a lot of the damage that Phil Goff caused
when he was Minister.
But the one thing I really do wish is this. You know, Phil Goff is always welcome to
come along to any def ence event; I always acknowledge him. But I wish he would just
behave the same way in the Chamber as he does at those events.
Vote agreed to.
Vote State Services agreed to.
Vote Foreign Affairs and Trade agreed to.
Vote Official Development Assistance agreed to.
Vote Sport and Recreation agreed to.
Vote Corrections

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.role: Chairperson of the Law and Order Committee
items.text: I am very
pleased to stand up and take a call on Vote Corrections. In fact,  I forgo the opportunity
to speak on another extremely well -performing department, and that is the police
department, to have an opportunity to speak on corrections, because I want to extend
my congratulations not only to the Minister of Corrections, Anne Tolley, but to the
Chief Executive of the Department of Corrections, Ray Smith, on turning round, over
the past 6 years —and I know the personnel have changed a little over that time, but
those are the people at the helm now —a service that is very, very str ongly focused on
reintegration and rehabilitation.
If I look back to when National first came into Government and look at corrections,
we used to see corrections officers occasionally along Lambton Quay in their ghastly
green, ill-fitting uniforms. That i s what they had for a number of years under a Labour
Government. I remember seeing the women officers walking along Lambton Quay,
wearing their uniforms with pride, but clearly their uniforms had not been cut for the
female figure. In fact, what they were having to do was wear uniforms that were not fit
for purpose. Well, no wonder they had extremely low morale within the corrections
service. The very first thing that the Minister of Corrections at the time did was give
them a new uniform, a new uniform tha t not only was fit for purpose but also
engendered the feeling of pride, and for the first time in many years, under this National
Government corrections personnel were not the scapegoat. They were no longer the
people who were blamed for anything that went wrong in corrections.
In fact, the culture has changed so significantly that all we ever see when we go on
prison visits are men and women who are professional and have absolute pride in their
work. They absolutely know they have been backed by their ch ief executive and their
Minister, and they have the strongest focus. They say it in their literature. They say it in
their book on reducing reoffending by 25 percent. They say that their absolute goal,
their ultimate goal, is to reduce reoffending. Well, what a change—what a change. What
a sea change that has been over the past 6 years under this National Government. We
have people who take pride in their work and have an absolute focus on reducing
reoffending.
That is based on some pretty significant rese arch that shows that when offenders are
released back into society, which, of course, they must be within months or even weeks
from their release from prison or in starting a community -based sentence, they then
reoffend pretty quickly. So it might be a mat ter of days; it might be a matter of hours.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19167
There is a tendency to reoffend. But also there is research that clearly demonstrates that
treatment programmes provided for within corrections facilities can change the attitudes
of prisoners and the beliefs of prisoners, and they can also teach them skills to cope on
the outside. So based on that knowledge, based on that understanding, based on the
great morale and great leadership in corrections, we now have a modern corrections
system that is absolutely focuse d on tackling drug and alcohol abuse. Most prisoners
who go into prison have issues around drugs and alcohol. We know that. We are
providing more rehabilitation to every prisoner and we are beginning to show, with the
prison muster and the rate of reoffend ing, which is dropping, that those rehabilitation
measures are working.
We have more interventions by probation staff. Probation staff are talking to
corrections staff and talking to the police, and together, with that combined effort, those
interventions are keeping prisoners from reoffending. There is now an out -of-gate
service in our corrections facilities. No longer do you have the day when prisoners
finish their sentences and literally walk out the gate and are left to their own devices.
Now strategies and plans are put in place to keep the prisoners safe, to keep them from
reoffending and renewing that useless, worthless cycle of crime, reoffending, and going
back into the corrections service.
One of the most memorable occasions I have seen over my time involved in law and
order was at the women’s prison in Wiri, where we went into a working kitchen and
spoke to a number of the women prisoners. They had huge pride in what they were
doing. They were not only catering for the construction crew for the men’s prison in
Wiri but also learning great skills that were transferable to the outside. Those prisoners
were looking to a life that did not involve crime any more.
Vote agreed to.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.
Vote Police

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I appreciate the opportunity to speak briefly to the
estimates debate on the police. I want to start by pointing out that in all of our debates
on the Budget, the Labour Party has been qui ck to highlight that our hope was for a
Budget that would set out a strong vision for work, for family, and for housing, because
those are all of the areas where we desperately need a strong vision for New Zealanders.
But underneath all of that, of course,  are the fundamentals; the things that of course
central government is involved in. Justice and law and order underpin whether or not
our families feel secure in their homes and their communities.
One of the things that I feel frustrated by in the police portfolio is that the Minister of
Police has started to take for granted, I think, that the basis on which she funds police is
her determination as to where the crime rate sits. Of course crime in New Zealand is
recorded crime. The rates that we use, that we talk about, are all based on whether or not
the general public are phoning in and reporting crime to the police. In order for people
to continue to do that, it relies on people feeling like that is a worthwhile venture, that
their report will be respond ed to, and that they will get some kind of either attendance
by police or some resolution to the issue that they have raised. So it does become a self -
fulfilling prophecy. If the police do not attend, someone is less likely to report, and
therefore it looks like your crime rate is going down.
We raised this at the Law and Order Committee during the estimates with the
Minister. She claimed that my view, and to raise this issue, was very last century. I
thought that was curious given it is an issue that memb ers of the public themselves have
raised. She claimed, for instance, that for property offences, of course someone would
phone in and report something because they require it for their insurance claim, ignoring
19168 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
completely the fact that we actually do not k now how many New Zealanders have
contents insurance. In all likelihood, I imagine, members of our poorer communities
may be less likely to have contents insurance and yet are more likely to be preyed upon
when it comes to things like property theft. So I d o not believe, Minister, that it is a
strong foundation to argue that based on all of those premises and the crime rate we can
therefore reduce our resourcing of policing.
In fact, it is not just in the operational budget, because in this Budget we have s een a
decline in the police budget by $40 million. It is a $40 million reduction —and that is on
top of frozen budgets and cuts —in operating expenditure for the police. The Minister
tried to claim that it was not actually a cut in funding; the Government ju st was not
putting in the extra boost it put in last time. Let me explain what that extra boost was. It
was a supplementary appropriation. Mid -year the Government realised that it had not
given the police enough to do the job and so it had to put a little bit of extra sneaky
money in through supplementary appropriations. The Minister claims those are costs
that we will not be facing again. They were basic costs like redundancy —redundancy
that was occurring, mind, to try to get police costs down.
We are in a vicious cycle with our police at present and we can see the impact it is
having. Example one is ageing police cars. We have now 71 vehicles that failed their
warrants of fitness in the last year, and 58 vehicles have done over 200,000 kilometres. I
have heard of police vehicles breaking down on the job. These vehicles are a key part of
the police doing their job. Not only is it an ageing fleet, they have got fewer cars since
this Government came into office.
Example two, we are seeing the police having to make cost-cutting priorities between
drug squads and reallocating people to child protection teams. Those are not two areas
that you should pick and choose between. Demand does not lift and drop when it comes
to serious organised crime and child protecti on. In fact, if anything, both of those areas
are escalating, and we need to maintain our focus on both.
Finally, staffing numbers—they are lower now than they were even 2 years ago. This
was the Government that in 2008 promised New Zealand a ratio of one police officer
per 500 people. The Minister conceded at the select committee that they have given that
promise away. They no longer retain that commitment. Why? Because apparently
everything is going swimmingly. Ask New Zealanders whether they think crime is
going down. Ask them. I think they will tell you that from this high -profile, serious
violent crime we are seeing, it certainly has not.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I woul d be very interested if we did
indeed ask New Zealanders whether they thought that crime was going down, because
public trust and confidence in the police is at an all -time high. The reality out on the
streets is that New Zealanders do know that things are going extremely well. Crime is at
a 35-year low. You do not make up those statistics. You cannot fiddle them. That is the
reality. Road fatalities are at a 60 -year low—down, down. Trust and confidence in the
police are up. In fact, when you have a look at  the engagement survey that the police
have an independent company do for them, staff engagement is at an all-time high.
So the police have never ever been in a better space. They are better resourced, they
are better focused, they are better managed, and  they have a better Government backing
them every inch of the way. They have come through 4 years of massive change. They
did it themselves. It was not driven by the Government. They knew that they had to
come out of 20th century policing into 21st century policing.
A lot of what we are hearing from the Opposition about numbers and about police
officers sitting in police stations waiting for people to come and report crime is very last
century. The modern police officer is in the right place at the right t ime with the right
tools and the right information. When we talk about them being in the right place, we
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19169
talk about them being out on the streets where people can see them. Foot patrols are up
by over 150 percent. We are having police out on the streets 15 0 times more. They are
being seen by people in the right places at the times when crime is happening. The
police are now focused on preventing crime rather than responding to crime. That does
not mean that if you are in trouble you cannot call the police, but they say that policing
is more about it being better to prevent crime happening in the first place, than to
respond to it and try to resolve it afterwards.
When we talk about them having the right tools, look at the smartphones and look at
the iPads that this Government has rolled out. There are 350 extra police officers’ worth
of technology that they can use. They are showing us how over the next 5 years to 10
years we are going to see a transformation in the way that evidence is kept and
presented. In fact I have seen it already, such as using FaceTime to record a drug deal
going down. There are amazing things that the police are finding that this new
technology will enable them to do.
When you talk about equipment now, they can start with the most i mportant tool that
they have, which is their tongues. You watch police go into some very dangerous
situations and the first thing they try to do is talk someone down, then they have their
batons, then they have pepper spray, then they have Tasers, and, fin ally, every police
car now has access to a Glock and to a Bushmaster rifle.
The police know this Government backs them. We are backing their district
command centres, which allow district commanders to look at where the need is right
across a whole distri ct and to move his or her resources around as the public’s need
dictates. That is modern policing. That is not 20 th century policing; that is modern
policing. We are allowing the police to get on and manage themselves so that we have
in this country one of  the most effective police forces in the world. We are the envy of
many other police forces in the world and we should be getting behind our guys instead
of trying to criticise these statistics and the work that the police are out there doing. We
should be backing them and saying that they are a tremendous group of people, who are
out there working with victims as the focus and preventing crime before it happens. I
am proud to be the Minister of Police.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Serious Fraud agreed to.
Vote Conservation agreed to.
Vote Housing

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Kia orana. This morning I
spoke with my electorate office. That is not unusual, you would argue, a nd, no, it is not,
but I spoke to my electorate office this morning about what is happening in housing and
particularly about what is happening with emergency accommodation in Christchurch. I
do that from time to time. The team down there lets me know what  is going on. We
keep records of people who come into the electorate office looking for assistance with
housing, particularly emergency accommodation providers. Today my team told me —
and I am just going to quote from the email they sent through to me today —that
currently there are no emergency housing units available in Christchurch. Further, it
went on to say that the Salvation Army is full and has waiting lists but cannot move
people on to permanent housing.
We all know that there is an issue with housin g in the Canterbury region, including
affordability, and affordability of rents. Our rents have moved over $100 a week in the
last year. We matched that to census figures that came out from One News a few days
19170 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
ago that said there have been 700 more people living in temporary dwellings and
overcrowded houses since the quakes. The census data also goes on to tell us there are
2,200 people in Christchurch living in temporary accommodation, up 50 percent from
2006, and 700 people living in mobile homes and make shift shelters. Overcrowding has
climbed, with more than 25,000 people living in crowded households.
We in Labour say that there is a better way —that the answer actually lies in building
more homes. To be fair, the Minister of Housing has done some work i n this regard.
The Christchurch housing accord with the Christchurch City Council will bring some
affordable rentals back into the market. But when I questioned the Minister—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: About time.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: That is right; it is way past time, actually, Ruth Dyson. When I
questioned the Minister at the select committee estimates discussion, he could not tell
me how many more affordable rentals the accord would bring, and nor could he tell me
when they were likely to  start construction. This Minister has really proved to be slow
in many areas. His own figures show that of the 700 new Housing New Zealand
Corporation homes he promised to build a year ago, he has built only 29.
From the Ministry of Social Development we  know that, of course, the number of
people who are on priority waiting lists for Housing New Zealand Corporation homes at
the last count was over 500. But, of course, we do not know what the new figures are,
because the Minister for Social Development has  not been able to provide us with any
figures since they moved the accessibility criteria to the Ministry of Social
Development in mid-April.
The Minister of Housing likes to quote consents as a measure of progress, and I
would just like to share some information about that as well. I have to say, to be fair,
that Christchurch is currently experiencing the highest number of consents ever. Well,
what a surprise that would be!

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Why?

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: I wonder why! I think they are supposed to be building houses,
are they not? The average number of consents for the period the National Government
has been in office, though, is 1,647. Let us compare that with the historic average of
1,926—this is annually—and compare it with the average of 2,012 over the years 1999
to 2008. This obviously goes to show that we were starting from some deficit even
before the quakes hit. That is significant, because we are starting from way back, past
left field, before we eve n consider how much we need to do to get us to pre -quake
levels.
The Minister says that the Canterbury region has to put up with housing
unaffordability for at least another 5 years. So for 8½ years people in Canterbury will
see their accommodation costs eat up more and more and more of their income. There is
a better way.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Kia orana, Mr Chair. Meitaki. I rise to take a call in
this estimates debate in regard to housing. I want to acknowledge my colleague over
there, Poto Williams, who talked about the issues of Christchurch and Canterbury. The
lessons from the Canterbury ea rthquakes are informing our work programme, which is
also focused on the provision of safe, healthy, and high -quality homes and buildings. I
just want to acknowledge some of the lessons that have been learnt from that, as well.
I think what is important i s that housing policy is one of the greatest challenges of
our time. It matters because most of our Kiwi families know that the equity in their
home is their greatest asset and that it has become increasingly difficult for families to
buy and own their own  home. I know that for myself. It was not, in fact, until my late
30s that my family and I were actually able to buy a home. I know how challenging and
how difficult it is, and the difficulty of that even in these times. That is one of the
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19171
reasons that this Government has embarked on a comprehensive package of reforms that
will make homes more affordable and reshape New Zealand’s approach to housing, as
well.
I also want to talk about some of the things that we are doing with regard to those
reforms. One of  the things we have done is the immediate suspension of anti -dumping
duties, through the Budget night legislation —duties on plasterboard, wire, nails, and
reinforced steel bars —for 3 years, from 1 July. The zero concessionary tariff is to be
reviewed after 5 years and covers around 90 percent of the materials in a new home. It
is expected to save $3,500 in the construction of a standard home. What I do know is
that, for me, for instance, coming from a construction background as an electrician —in
fact, I cou ld be one of the few tradespeople in Parliament —when constructing homes,
the cost of construction becomes critically important. One of the things I do know is
that when you compare the cost, for instance, of building in regard to square metreage,
the costs  in New Zealand are around $2,200 per square metre in comparison with
Australia’s, which are around $1,300. So if we can reduce those costs, we know the
difference that that can make; hence the issue of suspending tariffs is quite an important
one. We know the savings that that can make is around $3,500 in the construction costs
of homes.
The other thing we have done is put $64.3 million into new operating funding, new
capital funding, for social housing needs and functions for the Ministry of Social
Development. So the social housing sector also becomes quite critically important. We
know that in areas like Maraenui and Pōmare, and also over in Tāmaki, even with the
struggles they have had, they are very important.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: Do you know where Maraenui is?

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Yes, I do know where they are. I know that, for instance, the
Glen Innes housing project started off from going down to Maraenui and seeing what
was happening there—the work they had been doing in regard to engaging communities
about the issues of housing. So that was really important, as well. There are those of us
who do engage with communities as well. So what we did learn from that is the
importance of engaging in communities —in particular, around the so cial housing
sector. We know the importance of the role of the social housing sector; hence the
reason we have engaged with it.
A great project that has happened in our community—and you might not know about
it, Ms Whaitiri —is in Māngere. You might not kn ow where it is, but it is in Māngere.
There is a project called the Matanikolo Housing Project. It is a Tongan project that is
partnering with the Tongan community. They have this partnership where they have
been able to build 22 homes, so now the Tongan c ommunity has got this partnership
with Lifewise, a social housing provider, along with the Government. In that partnership
there is $4.3 million—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: How many times have we heard the same old story?

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Yes, you can go like that, but guess what? For all that talk, here
is a little bit of action that is really happening. And guess what is happening? This
Tongan community is saying for the first time that it has got a sense of participation and
ownership in  dealing with the housing issues for its community. It is a great project,
making a difference.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: It’s too slow.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Well, it may be slow where you come from, but I tell you what:
where we come from, over there in Māngere, they are absolutely celebrating it. They are
asking when the next project is. They are asking this Government when the next project
is so that we can partnership together. They have the land and they need some
opportunities. So our partnership with the social housing providers is absolutely making
19172 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
a difference. See, that is the difference between this Government and that potential
Government over there.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I came down to the Chamber to listen to
that excellent contribution from my colleague Poto Williams, but having had to sit
through Alfred Ngaro’s—how do I describe it? It was “inciteful” —it was an incitement
to disorder, listening to the blan d platitudes, the justifications of that member. That is
the member who claimed to come from Glen Innes in Auckland, but he has been the
worst—the champion, the apologist who justifies the disgraceful behaviour of Housing
New Zealand kicking out the elderl y, kicking out the disabled from homes they have
lived in for decades. He is the apologist for that sort of awful behaviour that even a
select committee unanimously criticised Housing New Zealand for. That member has
been the apologist for that kind of beh aviour. He stands there justifying the policies of
this National-led Government, which has done nothing about the housing affordability
crisis. That member stands up there like a pious vicar, justifying the complete failure of
the National Government’s housing policy.
There are no winners in the current housing crisis. Let us look at it. In Canterbury the
near-criminal negligence, the failure of this Government to actually get the residential
rebuild going, has seen fewer than 1,000 of the 12,000 to 15,000  houses that are needed
after the quake actually built after 3½ years. Mr Ngaro, the party that you stand up for
and justify in this Chamber is responsible for rents going up by more than 40 percent in
Canterbury and people living in sleepouts and sleeping  in cars. That is the policy that
you are proud of. In Auckland this Government has presided over skyrocketing house
prices. In the last year in Auckland house prices on average have gone up by $72,000
because of this Government’s total failure to do anyth ing meaningful about a
dysfunctional, failing housing market.
First-home buyers all over the country have been locked out of the dream of
homeownership by loan -to-value ratios of a 20 percent minimum deposit. If you are
earning the median wage in a place like Ashburton or Masterton of something like
$28,000 and you are paying tax on it, it is impossible to save the $60,000, $70,000, or
$80,000 deposit that you would have to have to even get in the door to talk to the bank
manager about a mortgage. But Alfr ed Ngaro would not know about that; he would not
care about that. He is too busy justifying the failure and inaction of this National -led
Government.
In the regions, because of this Government’s failure to crack down on speculators,
people are losing equi ty in their homes. In Southland in the last year the average house
price has gone down by $22,000. There is no housing crisis in Southland. It is because
of the failure of this Government to do anything about speculators in Auckland that
people in Southland—the other half of the population who do not live in Auckland and
Canterbury—are paying the price of that Government’s failure of a housing policy.
There are 285,000 kids living below the poverty line. More than half of those kids
are living in substanda rd private rental accommodation. But the best this Government
can do about it is a lame pilot scheme of its own State houses that it is too weak -kneed
to ensure are properly insulated and are warm and dry. Instead of doing something
about the private renta l market, where those kids are languishing in cold, damp homes
and ending up in hospital every winter, Nick Smith tries to look like he is doing
something by announcing a pilot scheme.
Alfred Ngaro talked about a comprehensive programme on housing. There is nothing
of the sort. What has this Government done in housing? The only thing it has got is a
lame housing accord in Auckland that has resulted in zero new houses being built a year
after that policy was announced. Not a single new house has been built in the special
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19173
housing areas as a result of that Government’s housing accord in Auckland. What a total
waste and a failure.
The Government has been talking about reforming the Resource Management Act to
speed up the consenting of residential development f or the last 6 years. We have got
something like 7 House sitting days left before the House rises, and it looks like it
probably will not even pass the legislation on reforming development contributions. It
has announced that it is not prepared—

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Well, we have just witnessed the
first election debate for the seat of Te Atatū between Mr Phil Twyford and Mr Alfred
Ngaro. In that debate we did see some a nger from Mr Twyford, so I think, given that he
is actually standing in a seat that is very much for the workers —and we are going to
pitch an electrician, a craftsman, versus an administrator —it is going to be a very
interesting battle in Te Atatū. But I w ant to focus on the positive work of this
Government—I very much want to focus on the positive work of this Government.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. There are members interjecting on each other who do not have the
floor. It is not permitted in the people’s House.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Housing New Zealand provides decent, affordable
housing to those who are most in need and when they need i t. It owns or manages
69,000 properties across New Zealand, housing around 200,000 people.
Today I want to acknowledge three people who have worked their guts out over the
last 9 years for my electorate in Napier. They are sitting in the gallery tonight: Tania
Wright, Vicki Sanders, and Sharon Coates. They have been my electorate agents over
the last 9 years. Unfortunately, they cannot come to my valedictory speech in a few
weeks’ time, but I just want to acknowledge the massive, massive work that they hav e
done over the last 9 years and throughout that period. Much of that work has been done
with Housing New Zealand and serving people who have walked in our door,
irrespective of whom they have voted for—that is not a question we ask when you walk
into my electorate office. They have been serving those people, helping them when they
are in tough situations and in a time of need, and working very closely, I might add,
with the fine people at Housing New Zealand. They have had to deal with many of the
changes that this Government has instituted over the last 3 or 4 years.
There have been some necessary things that we have needed to do with Housing
New Zealand. The facts are pretty simple. There are three things. Firstly, the
demographics have changed signifi cantly in terms of the requirements —what is
required in terms of the houses and the composition of those houses. Families have
changed, in terms of what is required. So what we have been supplying through
Housing New Zealand has not stacked up with those demographics.
Secondly, the quality of the housing in some cases —and in suburbs the likes of
Maraenui—has been appalling. If you look at the one-up, one-down homes, the side-by-
side homes that sit in that suburb, many of them that have not been pulled down  still
remain cold, wet, damp, and mouldy. They are a disgrace, quite frankly, and need to go
or be changed. The third thing, which has been the tough call that many in the House
have struggled with, but that we believe we need to get on top of, is some of  the
outcomes that proliferate around the cluster of those homes that are wet and damp and
terrible. Some of those outcomes are not pretty. Many in the likes of Maraenui have
very strong gang affiliations. That perpetuates all sorts of outcomes, including low
employment, low aspiration, and high crime levels even amongst and within the
community itself. In fact, some of the highest crime levels in the country occur most
repetitively within the lower socio -economic parts of the community. We make no
excuses for looking to change and to make changes. We are doing that.
19174 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
I have got to say I was proud just a few weeks ago to take the Prime Minister into
Maraenui and to take him to seven new homes that have been built in that wonderful
suburb—seven brand new home s. They are pitched right beside some of the one -up,
one-down homes —the cold, wet, and damp ones —that are now, fortunately, not
occupied any longer because they do not deserve to house people. But next door there
are seven new homes, and they achieved a si x-star rating. To put that into perspective, a
new, standard home built to current standards gets three to four stars. The one -up, one-
downs next door achieve only one star. They are a recipe for disaster, for illness, for
sickness, for bad health, and for  all sorts of things. Next door there are now seven
homes, which is the kind of stock that Housing New Zealand is now out there growing
around the country, with double glazing on the windows and insulation. I visited them
as they were being built. They have massive insulation on the ceiling.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Communications agreed to.
Vote Environment

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. I am very happy to take a call
on Vote Environment and al so the climate change aspects of the environment vote. I
think it is fair to say that the environment is going to be one of the major issues of this
election campaign. We have a Government that has a stated target of doubling
agricultural exports by 2025, but at the same time tells us that it wants to see no further
degradation of waterways. Well, I am sorry, I say to the Minister for the Environment,
but those two things do not go together. They cannot both happen. What we have is a
Government that is happ y to oversee further degradation of already very polluted
waterways in pursuit of an economic target that will inflict massive environmental
damage. It is a short -term sugar fix for people and farmers right now that will
potentially mean that future genera tions will not be able to farm land in the same way
that they do right now and that future generations will not be able to benefit from the
enormous environmental wealth on which our economy is based. That is what this
debate is about. It is about sustainability.
It is not about whether or not we farm; it is about how we farm and where we farm,
because what we know is that we are having land types with extremely vulnerable soils
being converted to dairying—lands that leech nutrients very quickly into waterways that
are already overallocated and already polluted. This Minister says that is fine. The
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment did a report earlier this year where
she talked about land use changes. For the first time, she brought together t wo
modelling tools that are well-known and that are very credible so that we could see what
land use changes would look like in 2020 and, therefore, extrapolate from that the
impact on waterways. What that showed was that with the settings the Minister has
suggested for the National Objectives Framework within the National Policy Statement
for Freshwater Management, the 2020 worst -case scenario that the Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment laid out in her report would not be stopped at all.
There is nothing in that National Objectives Framework that would stop the worst -case
scenario from happening.
That is of deep concern to a country that is not only hugely reliant on a healthy
environment—because I think Government members do not realise that w ithout a
healthy environment, we do not have a healthy economy. It is not a trade -off between
the two. We must protect our environment because without it, we have no economy. It
is as simple as that. It can be done. As I said, this is not about whether we farm; it is
about how we farm and it is about where we farm. That is a discussion that we should
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19175
be having, instead of, unfortunately, a proposed National Policy Statement for
Freshwater Management and a National Objectives Framework that will not stop further
extreme degradation of our waterways.
Labour has said that we will strengthen the National Policy Statement for Freshwater
