Management. We will bring back the national policy statement that we suggested when
we were in Government. We do not want to se e any further degradation of our
waterways, and we want to see remediation of those waterways that are already
polluted. But that is not what this Government wants to do.
So to compound it, what the Government has decided is that we need sweeping
Resource Management Act reforms. Apparently, it is the Resource Management Act
that is holding everything back. This is despite the fact that since 1991 our economy has
grown 75 percent—since the Resource Management Act was implemented. It has hardly
been held bac k by a piece of legislation that simply requires that the environmental
impacts of economic activity are taken into consideration and managed. That is what the
Resource Management Act does. That is what it is designed to do. It is not, and was
never meant to be, an economic development Act, yet that is what this Government
wants to turn it into. The Minister says it is failing. That is despite the fact that our
economy has grown by 75 percent since the Resource Management Act was introduced.
Our population has grown by 25 percent since the Resource Management Act was
introduced.
I note the most recent survey of local authorities in terms of their performance on the
Resource Management Act, and bear in mind the Minister says this is a broken system
that need s to be fixed. Do you know how many of the 34,000 consents that were
processed in the last financial year that was reviewed —and these reviews are done
every 2 years—were processed on time? Ninety -seven percent were processed on time.
Do you know how many w ere approved through this system that the Minister is trying
to convince New Zealanders is holding our economy back? Ninety -five percent were
approved. How many were appealed? It was 0.7 percent. How many were declined? It
was 0.27 percent. I think you wou ld struggle to find another piece of Government
legislation that is working as well as the Resource Management Act.
Labour agrees that process improvements can always be made to the Resource
Management Act and we have no issue with that, but we need to le ave the basic,
fundamental values—the heart and soul of the Resource Management Act —alone. We
have 20 years of case law that has been developed. If the Minister thinks that destroying
20 years of case law is going to provide certainty, then she is absolute ly off her rocker.
It will do nothing more than provide huge uncertainty and environmental degradation.
She has not actually shown or proved in any way that there is a problem that needs to be
fixed.
The Supreme Court has come to the rescue. In relation t o the recent New Zealand
King Salmon case, the Minister had been saying: “Well, the problem is, you see, the
values and the hierarchy of principles in the Resource Management Act are being given
a higher purpose in law than the national policy statements and planning documents like
regional plans and district plans. That’s the problem, so we need to amend Part 2 of the
Resource Management Act.” Well, Minister, you do not need to, because the Supreme
Court has just completely turned that on its head and said that, no, that is not the case. In
fact, those planning documents, where they use directive language, do have precedence
over Part 2 of the Resource Management Act. So rather than the Minister saying that
these are technical changes that will bring the Re source Management Act into line with
case law, case law and the Minister are now heading very quickly in completely
opposite directions—completely opposite directions.
19176 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
The Minister’s other argument is that the Resource Management Act is a sacred cow,
apparently—a sacred cow —that Opposition members are saying should never be
touched. How ridiculous! I asked the Parliamentary Library to do a search. There is no
other piece of legislation since 1991 that has been amended as many times as the
Resource Manageme nt Act. Barely 18 months have gone by without a Resource
Management Act amendment bill, and that is appropriate. What we need, however,
alongside it are the national policy statement and planning documents, which can guide
the Resource Management Act, stre amline processes, and provide far more central
government guidance. The Supreme Court has now given those planning documents a
supremacy that is extremely helpful.
I want to quickly come to the issue of climate change before my time runs out and
just say I am so disappointed with this Government’s performance on climate change.
This is actually about futureproofing our economy. We have to do this. This is not a
“nice to have”; this is something that we have to do. We have to transition away from
our heavy reliance on fossil fuels. The longer we leave it, the more difficult it becomes,
the more expensive it becomes, and we miss the amazing opportunities that are out there
right now. There are countries around the world that are crying out for low -carbon
solutions and crying out for low -carbon goods and services. This is our natural area.
This is our natural strength, and what are we doing? Nothing. In 2007 John Key said
that we need to be ahead of the game on this, that we need to realise that we will
become trading pariahs if we do not bring agriculture into the scheme, and that we need
to capitalise on the enormous potential and opportunities for New Zealand, as a country
that has—or used to have —an enormously high reputation in this area. We are being
overtaken by countries like Denmark, which is seeing these opportunities and rapidly
advancing towards it for the betterment of its economy.
The National Government says that it wants an emissions trading scheme but it does
not want a price on carbon. That is utterly ridiculous. Why would you have an
emissions trading scheme, the sole purpose of which is to price carbon, if you did not
want a price on carbon? Then the Government makes up some ridiculous figure that it
will cost $500 extra a year to have a proper price on carbon. That is utter garbage that is
being made up. Do you know what? If the Government had transparency around carbon
pricing and stopped the price -gouging that it knows is going on by electricity and fuel
companies, which would drop the price of carbon, actually the overall cost would not be
that much to businesses and households at all. Of course, what we are doing is
incentivising low-carbon products by giving them a price advantage. That is the point of
a price on carbon. The Government has  allowed cheap units to flood into our emissions
trading scheme, collapsing the price of carbon and damaging our forestry sector. That is
the one sector that did all the heavy lifting over the last 6 years. The only reason that we
came out positive in the first commitment period of the Kyoto Protocol and did not face
a massive bill was forestry. Our gross emissions kept going up. We were just planting
enough forests to more than mitigate that.
Well, in 2020 those forests come down, and because of the Gover nment’s climate
change policies, we are not replanting the forests. We will face a massive, massive bill.
If there is a post-2020 agreement, there is a real risk that it may be unaffordable for New
Zealand to enter that agreement—that is, if we do not do something about planting more
forestry and reducing our gross greenhouse gas emissions right now. Can you imagine
how devastating it would be for our reputation if the mess that this Government leaves
is so bad that we have to equivocate on whether or not w e are able to enter into a post -
2020 agreement? The Government’s climate change plan is 0.4 percent difference from
doing nothing at all.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19177
MAGGIE BARRY (Chairperson of the Local Governmen t and Environment
Committee): I rise to speak on Vote Environment in the Committee stage of the
Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill and I speak with great enthusiasm about our
environmental and conservation measures. The last speaker, Moana Mackey, outl ined
very clearly the great philosophical void and enormous divide that exists between our
two parties. I am passionate about the environment. I work for a Government that is also
passionate about the environment and does excellent and remarkable things to safeguard
it. That is why I joined National. That is why I approve, ultimately, of all of the
activities that our Minister for the Environment, Amy Adams, and our Minister of
Conservation, Dr Nick Smith, have put in place.
Let us take a few of the proposa ls and achievements that we are putting through over
the next little while, and there are a lot more to come. Expect some big announcement
about fresh water and ensuring good water quality in the lead -up to this election,
because that is something of an ab solute priority. I agree with what the Opposition
members say —it is a priority. Where we absolutely disagree is the way we want to
achieve it. We are not about rhetoric. We are not about mad words that promise lots and
deliver nothing. We are not about ped dling things that are absolutely impossible to
deliver. You cannot manage what you cannot measure. We measure it, we look it, and
we make policies that really do ensure that our freshwater resources, which are
precious, are replenishable. They are not unlimited though; we need to look after them.
There are no quick -fix solutions to the problems with our waterways. There is no
magic Labour wand or Green wish -it-were-so policy that will change the inevitable.
What we have done as a Government is to address t he substance and to put together
packages and clean -ups that will lead to a more productive and sustainable use of our
freshwater resources, not only for our farmers, whom I am sick of hearing being
demonised. Dirty dairying—really and truly, you start to lose the will to live when you
hear the way that people try, with captions and slogans, to demonise and vilify one
group in society. People are trying extremely hard to come up with practical solutions.
That is something that happens when you have a Minist er for the Environment who is
also a farmer, because she understands and knows the practical, day -to-day realities of
actually running a farm and dealing with it.
Let us look at some of the reforms that we have established to date. The Land and
Water Foru m—what an extraordinary thing. Imagine getting all the enemies of the
environment, climate change, and conservation all in one room, and that they talk
together. In the 9 long years of the Labour Government it was considered to be an
incredibly unlikely scenario and one not even worth trying. By 2009 we had formed the
Land and Water Forum, and, as Dr Nick Smith has done and has put some
extraordinarily good work into, we have managed to maintain a level of collaboration
where you do get together people who want the same thing, which is the betterment of
our environment. They come to the table and they give a little and they gain a little, and
they get the job done. That is what the Land and Water Forum has done.
Let us look at the stakeholders and the way t hey have done the groundbreaking
research. There probably is not actually time for me to go into the Land and Water
Forum’s achievements in any great detail, but look at the National Policy Statement for
Freshwater Management. That came in in 2011, and it gave councils a clear pathway
and a national direction, for the first time, on how to set limits to achieve water
management objectives. You need to be able to look at this sensibly and to take the
emotion out of the argument, and that is what has been don e. The development of that
National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management provided a robust, scientifically
backed set of attributes to help communities plan to meet their particular objectives.
Hold the front page —it is not that difficult an idea, bu t it is a concept that the
19178 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
Opposition parties seem unable to grasp. Maybe it is just politics, but we put that to one
side because the environment matters to us.
We have put about $101 million recently on to water clean -ups, and have committed
a further $ 350 million, which is a fivefold increase in funding, and that is just for lake
and river clean -ups. This is where it counts and this is where it matters. Put the empty
rhetoric aside. In the latest Budget a further $12 million in extra funding will be spe nt
over the next 4 years, again, to help councils and communities come together to plan
and make decisions about their own problems —looking local and using local solutions,
and working together with that breadth of knowledge. I have seen it recently with t he
Kaikōura (Te Tai -o-Marokura) Marine Management Bill. We had a collaborative
approach there, which has been done over —oh, I do not know —15 years in total, but
very seriously for the past 7 years. That is a workable solution that was ultimately
embraced by the Greens and by Labour, and the Supplementary Order Papers and the
debate, I guess, when the bill comes back to the House, will settle any points of
difference. We believe as a Government —this National, John Key-led Government—in
collaboration, and it works with the environment.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Vote Environment for 2014 -15
totals over $313 million and 61 percent of that relates to the Ministry for the
Environment’s climate change responsibilities, and my colleague Kennedy Graham will
comment on that. But 39 percent of the vote is for other aspects of environmental
management, and a significant chunk of that covers fresh water. The Ministry for the
Environment gets $14 million to provide advice and implement tools for water
management.
We live in a country that is shaped by more than 180,000 kilometres of rivers. Some
of them are deep and swift, and others, like the Waimakariri, have wide beds that spread
into many strands on the plains. Some, like the Tarawera, start in lakes, and others have
their headwaters in the snowfields of the Southern Alps. We New Zealanders love our
rivers. They inspire us with their beauty and power, as places to go fishing and
kayaking, as a source of  kai, or for their own sake. Nine high -profile New Zealanders,
including musicians Tiki Taane, Maisey Rika, artist Grahame Sydney, photographer
Craig Potton, and comedienne Michele A’Court, and 2,000 other New Zealanders have
signed an open letter to the e nvironment Minister calling on her to get tough on water
pollution. New Zealanders want the Minister and her ministry to introduce strong
standards to protect water quality and reduce the pollution load that intensive land use
puts on our rivers.
I under stand that tomorrow the Minister will release the Government’s final
decisions on the National Policy Statement on Freshwater Management. That national
policy statement is the major policy document under the Resource Management Act,
and it influences how o ur rivers, streams, lakes, and aquifers are managed and how
councils control land use that affects water quality. But National has no plan for clean
rivers. Under this Minister and this National Government, the Ministry for the
Environment has proposed wea k national bottom lines for water quality that will allow
more water pollution. We have got high limits on pollutants such as nitrogen and faecal
coliform. Why? So that irrigation and dairy intensification can continue to expand.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Why do you talk such nonsense?

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Mr Finlayson is interjecting. Mr Finlayson, last November when
National released the proposed changes to the national policy statement, they were
widely criticised. Th e Fish and Game Council said the national bottom lines for water
quality would allow New Zealand rivers to become some of the most polluted in the
OECD. It described them as an abject failure that, in its words, legitimised the worst
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19179
farm nitrate pollution  we have in New Zealand now and allowed water pollution to
increase by five to 15 times over current levels.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: Who said that?

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: It was not just the Fish and Game Council; it was also the
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment. She said that the National Objectives
Framework did not go far enough to address the most widespread, pervasive, and
immediate pressure, which is the rapidly increasing nutrient loads from land use change.
In the last 5 y ears the amount of irrigated land in New Zealand has increased by an
area the size of Lake Taupō and Lake Te Ānau combined. An extra 60,000 hectares in
Canterbury have been irrigated, covering an area the size of Lake Taupō. The
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, Parliament’s environmental
watchdog, wants the Government to increase the measures in the national policy
statement so that regional councils regulate land use change to prevent more nutrient
leaching, more faecal contamination, and mo re water pollution. But National prioritises
irrigation development and intensive land use over rivers that are clean enough to swim
in. There is no limit to the novel food products and the jobs we can create if we use our
intelligence, if we focus on rese arch and development, and if we add value to the milk
we currently produce, but there is a limit on the number of dairy cows we can put on the
land. The Green Party recognises this; National does not. In areas like Lake Taupō we
have reached that limit.
More than 90 percent of the 7,000 submitters on the Government’s proposed changes
to the national policy statement called for a health standard that ensured that rivers were
clean enough to swim in. The Green Party would introduce standards that provided th at.
When the Minister announces her changes tomorrow, I would love to see a change in
that standard to ensure that our rivers are clean enough to swim in, but given that
National prioritises irrigation, I doubt that we will see that.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: It is a great privilege to take
a call on Vote Environment in the estimates debate for this year. I think that the
National Government can stand here incr edibly proud of what we have done in the
environment space in the last year. I am happy to go toe to toe with anyone in this
Parliament on our actual record. Leaving aside all the hand -wringing rhetoric and the
tired old clichés and the thinly veiled hatre d of farmers that those members hide under
their rhetoric, in actual action on the ground this is a Government that has delivered in
every single component that makes up the environment portfolio.
We have heard a lot about fresh water, but what I can tell  you is this. This is the
Government that put in place a National Policy Statement on Freshwater Management.
This is the Government that is going to introduce for the first time nationally required
bottom lines. This is the Government that required regiona l councils to make sure that
water quality is always maintained or improved. This is the Government that spent five
times what the previous Government spent on water clean -ups. This is the Government
that required for the first time metering of large irrig ation consents. This is the
Government that is putting this country on a path to cleaner, better, more sustainable
fresh water.
But here is the difference. This is also a Government that recognises that New
Zealanders want jobs, they want a high standard of living, and they want all the things
that the taxes from our productive sector pay for. So we are not going to do it in a way
that kills the golden goose. We are not going to slam the door on business. We are not
going to demonise anyone who commits the  unforgiveable sin of actually running a
business, being profitable, and creating a job. We are going to say: “Let’s do it in a way
that achieves both.”
19180 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
Unlike the Labour speaker Moana Mackey, who said that you absolutely could not
have clean water and in crease agriculture, we do not accept that. We believe that you
can. In fact, we know you can. We have seen it happening. New Zealand farmers, New
Zealand business people, and New Zealanders as a whole are the most innovative, the
most clever, and the most creative people in the world, and they are already adapting
and they are already showing that you can absolutely farm in a way that is more
profitable, that is more successful, and that significantly reduces their environmental
impact. That is what we back  and that is absolutely what we are going to see happen.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Sorry to interrupt the
Minister. It is happening ag ain. Members who do not have the floor and who interject
on each other because they have a disagreement —that is not permitted in the people’s
House. If you want to interject, then you can interject on the speaker on my right, but
not on each other.

items.speaker: Hon AMY  ADAMS
items.text: That same approach of talking one game and then not
following through is seen throughout Labour’s approach. So let us look at the Resource
Management Act. Again we heard Moana Mackey railing against this, but here is what I
would say. If the Labour Party wants to go to the electorate on a platform that there is
nothing wrong with the Resource Management Act, bring it on. Bring it on, because I
can tell you that every single public satisfaction survey that is done on how the public
find our services across national and local government consistently rates the Resource
Management Act not only as a fail but as having the lowest rating of every single
service. So if Labour wants to campaign against us on the basis that the Resource
Management Act is working really well and we are happy with it, I welcome it.
Again, here is the difference. We understand that our planning laws absolutely have
to protect our environment. They absolutely have to care about the water, the soil, and
the air that we all enjoy and need in order to live. But also we recognise that people care
about jobs, houses, and infrastructure. Labour suggests that our planning laws are not
even allowed to make reference to the importance of land for housing, or the importance
of creating new economic growth opportunities, and it then has the audacity to come to
this Committee and say: “Where are the jobs and what are you doing about housing?”,
when it has blocked every single opportunity in this House to back us on sensible
reform that would put things like housing, infrastructure and natural hazard
management—that is all we want to put in it —right at the heart of the Resource
Management Act. But, according to the Opposition, you are allowed to ask only
whether there will be any negative impact. That is all you are allowed to ask. Never
mind that people actually need houses to live in. They need houses to live in, and this
Government recognises it.
Let us have a look at the exclusive economic zone. Here is another great example,
right? The exclusive economic zone. What happened under Labour and the Greens?
They drilled as many holes as they wanted out there, and do you know what the process
was? Their energy Minister signed it off. That is it. That was the entire economic and
environmental assessment —one energy Minister signed it in his office. Under the
National-led Government we have, for the first time, a strong environmental impact
assessment before anything can happen in our exclusive economic zone. And for all the
people on the Opposition benches who screamed that this was some sham, rubber-stamp
process, how is that looking now? We have a strong, independent, very detailed
oversight of anyone who wants to operate in our exclusive economic zone. Yes, we do
want to see development, but only if they can meet that very high threshold. It is a high
bar—
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19181

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chairman. This is a Government
whose 2014 estimates contain a time bomb of fiscal deficit over the next two decades
through a failure in carbon budgeting. This is a Government whose climate change
policy is a mess. It has paltry targets with no plan to attain them. It has weak policy
settings, so emitters have no incentive to change, and that, I say to the Minister for the
Environment, will kill the golden goose. But even worse is the failure to convey to the
taxpayer the fiscal costs that its  climate policy will impose on future generations. The
emissions trading scheme under current settings aspires to manage fiscal risk primarily
through forestry, and the harvesting of trees is therefore fully priced. But the impact of
the emissions trading scheme on other sectors is softened by compensation, the gifting
of units, and the exclusion of an entire sector that makes up half of our emissions.
In 1992 New Zealand undertook to reduce emissions. Since then its emissions have
soared and are projected  to continue to do so out to 2050. What is the fiscal effect of
that? New Zealand has committed to three emission targets: 2008 -12, 2020, and 2050.
By drawing straight lines between these targets, the Government sets a primitive kind of
national carbon bud get. It calculates the annual emissions within those lines and then
compares the limits with the projected emissions to find the excess. For the period
2013-50, Treasury projects that under current policy settings, excess emissions will total
around about 1 billion tonnes of emissions. Net emissions will more than double the
Government’s target in 2050.
One way or another, this excess has to be paid for. This Government refused to enter
a binding commitment under Kyoto II, so we face no financial penalty i f we fail and
exceed our 2020 target, but after 2020 there will certainly be an international carbon
price of some kind, and it will rise fast. It cannot be otherwise. The British climate
commission assumes that international prices will rise from about US $50 to US$150 a
tonne during that decade. There will be a binding obligation on emission limits by then,
and a financial penalty of some kind for exceeding them. At US$25 a tonne, the external
carbon budget deficit for New Zealand will amount to maybe US$3 0 billion. Imagine
the fiscal hurdles for the next generation, when we might be paying up to six times that
price.
In 2 months voters choose which party will govern for the next 3 years. They have
two considerations: security for themselves and a future f or their kids. This is a
Government that flaunts a reduction of current account deficit next year and ignores the
future. But the fiscal debt from current climate change policy will be simply
horrendous—a major financial haemorrhage in the 2020s. Because o ur accounting
methods are inadequate, this is hidden from the taxpayer and the voter. The principle of
carbon responsibility is lost on this Government. The Public Finance Act requires the
Government to manage fiscal risk with prudence. How is the public g oing to judge the
Government on that basis?
This is a Government that misrepresents the facts to the public. Over the past month
it has derided the Green Party’s proposal for a carbon tax, claiming that our tax would
be five times the global price. What p ure rubbish! There is no single global price; there
is a range of international prices. So how does the Green price level compare? The
Green proposal is for US$22 a tonne for carbon dioxide and US$11 for biological
emissions. So how does this compare with international prices? Well, there is China,
Quebec, California, and France at US$10, then there is the UK at US$16, Australia at
US$22, Finland at US$48, Switzerland at US$68, Tokyo at US$95, and Sweden at
US$168. So our proposal sits very comfortably with in the carbon price range overseas.
This is a Government whose estimates, along with its spin, are misleading, tendentious,
and dangerous.
Vote agreed to.
19182 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
Vote Primary Industries

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: It is great to take a call in
this debate on the appropriations. I want to say what a fantastic year it has been for
primary industries. Just in the last couple of weeks we have released a document,  the
Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries 2014 , which records that our primary
sector is in boom times—a nearly $38 billion return. Is that not fantastic?

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why are you ripping off farm workers?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Andrew Little chips in. He would not know one end of a cow
from the other, even though he is standing in the New Plymouth electorate. Labour does
not care about the rural communities. I want to take Andrew Little and Labour and the
Green Party through why the primary sector is so vitally important to the New Zealand
economy. As I was saying, $38 billion was returned from our exporters in our primary
industries this year. Is that not fantastic? Dairy is up to around $17 billion. Meat and
wool are up  to and through $8 billion, which is fantastic, and is forecast to return 22
percent out to 2018. Then, of course, we have the forestry sector. There are boom record
times for it—$5.1 billion. Horticulture is going strongly, with $3.6 billion in terms of its
exports. It is forecast to go to $4 billion by 2016. And we should not forget about our
seafood exporters, who do a fantastic job of producing a quality product that goes all
around the world, at $1.45 billion.
But, of course, we cannot have a big -growth target of doubling our exports to $64
billion by 2025 without focusing on protecting our primary industries, and that is why I
am excited about Vote Primary Industries. It is strengthening the core systems for
biosecurity and for food safety. We are put ting more resources into our overseas
footprint. I want to talk specifically about biosecurity because it is my No. 1 priority as
Minister for Primary Industries. We have doubled the funding since 2000 in biosecurity,
and there is more funding in this Budg et. What we have also done is roll out 12 new X -
ray machines. We have trained more front -line quarantine inspectors—125 were trained
in the last 18 months, including new dog detector teams. What we have also done is
introduce Government -industry agreements , and we have had the first signing of the
deed with the kiwifruit industry.
What we have also done in just the last few weeks is announce $65 million for a new
biocontainment facility at Wallaceville in the Hutt Valley. It has gone down
fantastically well with those in the primary sector because they know that we need to
have our testing regime up to international best practice. They know that $20 billion
worth of animals and animal product exports is the result of our farmers and the
fantastic work that they do. This is the insurance premium and policy for the next 30
years for our primary sector —to know that we have world -leading and best -practice
scientists doing the testing for exotic animal diseases.
The other important thing is, of course, that we h ave the opportunity to grow Māori
agribusiness in New Zealand. We did a study about a year and a half ago that confirmed
that 1.5 million hectares in New Zealand is Māori freehold land, and the opportunity for
Māori to work closely with the Government to l ift their overall performance is huge.
We are talking about $8 billion in terms of export returns, and we are talking about
3,600 jobs.
The Green Party and Labour do not like talking about irrigation because they do not
believe in it. They do not believe i n rural communities. They do not believe in jobs and
exports, but we on this side of the Chamber do. We believe that irrigation is good.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Subsidies.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: We believe that irrigation is good, and I will tell you why. Mr
Shearer might be interested in this, because he would not understand rural communities.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19183
There are 400,000 hectares of land that could be under irrigation that is not under it
currently, and the size of the prize here is $4 billion. The  other important thing about
irrigation is that it is good for the environment, and the reason it is good for the
environment is that you take the pressure off the aquifers. You can store water —we
collect and store only 2 percent of the water in this count ry; the other 98 percent goes
into the streams and rivers and heads out to sea —and we have got numerous cases up
and down the country, particularly in the South Island, where, as a result of irrigation,
rural towns have been repopulated and schools have be nefited, as have businesses and
the New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.role: Chairperson of the Primary Production Committee
items.text: Thank
you for the opportunity to contribute in this debate. It is interesting to follow on from
the Minister for Primary Industries, who talked about the opportunities coming from
irrigation. If you had been listening earlier to the debate on the estimates for
environmental portfolios, you would have though t that this was going to be the end of
the environment in New Zealand, when, in fact, the opposite could not be more the case
if you look at science, and, of course, we are asking people to look at science —which is
a step too far for, more or less, two-thirds of the Opposition, as far as I can tell.
We are asking people to look at actual scientific evidence, and the reality is this.
When irrigation was developed in the upper part of the South Island, in the Kaikōura
and Nelson regions, during the late 1970s  and early 1980s, large amounts of land were
developed for viticulture. So I guess what we are saying is that those grapevines should
go and that land should revert back to what was there prior to the pinot and the
sauvignon blanc being planted, and then we would be in a much better position, because
the automatic presumption is that if you irrigate land, it is all going to go into dairying.
That, in itself, would not be a bad thing, because there is plenty of technology now to
mitigate the types of environmental effects that they talk about. In fact, if they had gone
to the Fieldays—and I invite the Green Party to look at this technology—and had a look
at some of the new innovation that was on display there in regard to environmentally
sustainable use of la nd and water, they would not hold this Luddite position that they
have.
So let us just have a look at what actually has been achieved in the dairy sector, in
the primary industries area, in the last wee while. The Dairying and Clean Streams
Accord—87 perc ent of the streams, rivers, and lakes and 90 percent of the races, or
access ways, for cattle have now been fenced and bridged. No other industry has
achieved that, in that time. Ninety -nine percent of dairy farms have nutrient budgets. I
am not asking those who are in the Chamber to understand what that means, but what it
basically means is that all nutrients that are applied are budgeted for and calculated
against what is used. It is not very hard to understand. There is a warrant of fitness
system for dairy effluent management, which is controlled both by the regional councils
and the dairy companies that they supply. Dairy effluent non -compliance is less than 10
percent nationally and coming down. It is substantially reducing each year.
There is research  for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, based on science once
again, and New Zealand’s investment in this area is world -leading. Why do we not hear
the Greens or Labour touching on that from time to time? Dairy companies are
implementing stringent criteria in terms of their supply regimes.
Why do we not hear from the Labour members, who I know are passionate about
increasing wages, about what has actually happened in terms of dairy worker wage
limits or wage rises in recent times? Why do we not hear about t he stories of young
couples now in that sector who are earning $130,000 —what they call the total value
package? Why do we not hear about that? The majority of them, in the larger operations
19184 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
in a mid-management position, are earning that money and more, and  some are earning
up to $300,000 and $400,000. When do we hear about that? When does the Green Party
talk about that?
Why do we not hear about the massive investment that is going on in local
communities in philanthropic ways, through the likes of milk in  schools, for example—
that is one starting point—as well as all the local investment that goes on in small towns
and communities in regard to philanthropic activity? It is all driven on the back of
investment in our primary sectors.
Why is it that we cons tantly hear the negative carping in the background from our
Opposition? Why do we not start celebrating the areas that we are good in? Why do we
not get over the fact that we are an agricultural nation and we depend on our agricultural
sector? Seventy-two percent of our export earnings come from the agricultural sector. I
cannot help it if two-thirds of the members in this House do not like that —I cannot help
it—but it does not change the fact. If they do want to develop something else to replace
it, please do. But let us not pretend there is some silver bullet. This is a sector that will
grow the New Zealand economy faster than any other sector.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I want to say that this is the first year I
have not been to Fieldays. I have been to it for the past 4 years. I can tell you that the
same thing happens to me every time I go there. Somebody will come up to me and say:
“You know, we in the rural sector always do b etter under Labour.” They always say
that. I am telling you, this is what people say. I say to them: “Well, why don’t you vote
Labour?”. “No, no, I still vote National.” I do not get it, but, anyway, that is what they
tell us.
There are a lot of people wh o have been sitting here, if they have not gone to sleep
listening to the last two speakers, and who are in front of their TVs waiting for that cold
spell to come up New Zealand. They are thinking about whether they will have to turn
up their heaters a lit tle bit more in order to stay warm. A lot of them are thinking: “I’m
not sure whether I can afford to do that.” The power prices, they know, have gone up 20
percent—20 percent—in the last 4 years under a Government that said it was going to
bring those pow er prices down. That is four times faster than inflation —four times
faster than inflation—that power prices have been going up.
Here is the interesting thing about that. When Labour was in power —and, yes, I
agree that power prices went up then —the demand for power was rising at an ever -
increasing—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! We are actually on Vote Primary
Industries.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Are we? I thought he was talking about energy.

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: We use electricity, though.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: So you want to put the motion, do you?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Yes, so the member has just lost a call,
unfortunately, because we are on Vote Primary Industries, and I think the member
was—

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Can I carry on, on primary industries in relation to energy?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: You can talk about primary industries.
Otherwise you have just lost the call, because what you have done is you have actually
taken a call. I am happy for you to continue, but you must relate it to primary industries.

items.speaker: DAVID SH EARER
items.text: The thing about these power prices going up is that it is
affecting farmers right across the country. In every dairy shed, in every processing
plant, these farmers are being affected by electricity prices going up at four times the
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19185
rate of inflation. It is not just the urban areas; it is the rural areas. It is affecting the
farmers, who are the backbone of this country. They are being hit harder than anybody
else. This is Economics 101. When demand falls, prices should fall, but, inst ead,
farmers all across New Zealand, throughout the rural sector, are paying more for their
electricity than they ever have before.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Let’s be honest. You wouldn’t have a clue.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Do not interrupt me, Mr Bridges.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Let’s be honest.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Let us be honest? That would be a change —that would be a
change—because today all we have heard is the exact opposite of that. Your Minister of
Foreign Affairs stood up and told a whole lot of rubbish about what has been going on.
I come back to the rural community. Farmers deserve to have transparency around
their power bills. They want to know how much of their power being delivered is being
charged to them from the electricity companies and how much is being charged to them
from the lines companies. In that member’s area many of those lines companies are
coming to people and saying that they are paying too much, when it is actually the
electricity companies in those members’ electorates, in those rural areas, that depend so
heavily on funding.
What have we got? We have got falling demand and rising prices that are hitting the
farming community right across New Zealand. Sixty percent of our power i s coming
from hydroelectricity generated in some of those farming and rural areas—60 percent of
power is coming from there. We have paid for those dams over and over, and yet we are
still paying far more for our electricity than just about anywhere else in  the Western
World.
We are just asking for a fair deal —we are just asking for a fair deal. People are
sitting at home right now watching this debate on television, thinking twice about
turning up their heater in order to stay warm, and knowing that if the y do their power
bill will be through the roof. I feel for them, because this Government has raised those
prices four times faster than inflation, at a time when demand for electricity is falling. If
you know anything about economics, that is absolutely wrong. Thank you.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I rise to speak on Vote Primary Industries
mostly in response to hearing what seemed to be waffle from the Government side. I
was going to speak on food safety because of the shortfalls in food safety and the many
things that that Minister for Food Safety is not doing —and should be doing —in her
role, but we will come back to that.
The Minister spoke clearly about his priority in biosecurity, and I commend  him for
having that as a priority. But what I am not seeing is real delivery in biosecurity. What
we are seeing are things that make us still very, very nervous in terms of incursions into
this country. Inspections are way, way too low. Containers once we re inspected, right
round them. Containers are now maybe inspected on four sides of them, and then it is
random enough at that, although it is based on an improving system through the joint
work of the Customs Service and Ministry for Primary Industries.
The problem is that we then allow retailers, wholesalers, and importers to inspect
their own containers, and how crazy is that when those same people have a conflict of
interest? They have got a vested interest in having the goods out of that container and
out on to the shelves in shops and things. If they see something, are they going to report
it to the Ministry for Primary Industries? And even then, is the Ministry for Primary
Industries going to do a decent job?
I have mentioned to the Minister before about theileria, a particular strain of theileria.
This Government allowed this cattle disease to get loose, which is costing millions, and
it will cost millions for ever because it allowed the disease to get loose and to spread. At
19186 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
the same time, Governme nt members were chortling that they are ready for foot -and-
mouth disease, should it come here. That was a prime example of what they might have
used to actually test their systems. They have no reason to be confident. New
Zealanders have no reason to be co nfident that they can really control foot -and-mouth
disease, should it come here.
I am pleased there is more and more work being done on it, and the report expresses
that. But there was a prime opportunity to jump on a very —how shall I say —effective
protozoan parasite in cattle and use that as an example. What have we got the National
Animal Identification and Tracing system for, if you could not use that for animal
controls and to get on top of that pest? That happened within this Parliament, and this
Minister has to share some of the blame for that. That one is just one.
But one that also concerns me is another part —the genetic engineering in some
laboratories. That is where we think genetic engineering should be, but there was a
breach—and the breach wa s back in early 2013 —of a genetically modified fungus out
of Lincoln University. But it is the Ministry for Primary Industries that has the
responsibility for monitoring and making sure these facilities are working within the
constraints of their condition s. We have been chasing the information on the report of
the investigation on that for so, so long, and the Minister has ducked and dived and tried
not to supply it. I wonder why? The report showed that for 3 years Lincoln University
had inadvertently got GE fungus and was even potentially putting it out into apple
orchards and Pinus radiata nurseries in this country because it has been poorly supplied
by AgResearch.
It is the Ministry for Primary Industries that has failed in monitoring and keeping an
eye on that. Can we trust the Ministry for Primary Industries and the current Minister,
and this current Government, to be doing better than this? We still have not got the final
report on this released. Have we got confidence? No, we have not got confidence
because they have not been able to supply the report to the people who are caring about
it, the people who are very, very concerned. The research was fine. The research had
good intent.
Vote agreed to.
Vote Commerce and Consumer Affairs agreed to.
Vote Energy agreed to.
Vote Labour

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a great pleasure to take a call on this very
important part of the estimates. It was, frankly, a bit rich when the various farming or
former farming members opposite stood before the Committee, under a different vote a
short while ago, to boast about the great achievements in the farming sector and the
great wealth being generated in that sector for this great country of ours. But they did
not mention one thing about the role that the Minister of Labour played in ensuring that
farm workers on the minimum wage now get paid less than the minimum wage for 1
week out of every fortnight on their “12 and 2” work roster.
What a disgraceful action by the  Minister of Labour. What a shameful thing by this
Government. Government members say they like the rural sector. They say they look
after people in the rural sector and in the provinces. They do not give a damn about the
hard-working people—the hard-working people who are out there early in the morning,
doing the milking, doing the hard graft on the farms, putting up the fences, getting a
tractor out, doing the feeding-out in the bitter cold weather that we have at the moment.
This Government does not care  a toss about those people, and it quite happily reduces
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19187
their wages because it wants to please the big, wealthy, rich farm owners. Well, it is
shocking. It is shocking, and it is the farm labourers who are turning up to the offices of
Labour MPs, saying: “What gives? What’s going on?”. What possible law could there
be that allows a Minister, at the stroke of a pen, to take $100 a fortnight off hard -
working farm labourers? What a shocking thing.
Well, the truth is this. We might have a Minister of Labour, but we have an
appallingly dysfunctional labour market at the moment —46 percent of hard -working
New Zealanders cannot get a pay rise in a single year alone, and 49 percent of
employers in a survey last week said they will not give a pay rise to their staff  this year.
And yet, members opposite sit in the chair, they stand opposite, and they crow about the
great economic growth. It was 3.2 percent a year about 3 months ago. Now it is up to
3.8 percent. Who knows how big it will be in a couple of months’ time when they are
on the hustings.
But here is the catch. We have a great growing economy —some people are doing
well; some people are doing extraordinarily well —but 46 percent of hard -working New
Zealanders cannot get a pay rise, and the Minister does not car e. The Minister does not
care. He is the Minister of Labour. One of his prime responsibilities is to make sure that
we have a wage -setting system and that people are fairly rewarded. That is what we
expect in a properly functioning labour market. But we ha ve a Minister who does not
care that half the workforce cannot get a decent pay rise, and that half of employers are
saying they are not going to pay any more. So we are in a pretty diabolical situation.
We know that the income gap is getting worse. We know that inequality is getting
worse in this country. We now have the lowest level of homeownership since 1951
because people cannot afford houses. Housing affordability is not just an issue about
house pricing; it is about wages and incomes, and wages an d incomes in this country
have been getting worse and worse for a larger and larger number of people. It is getting
worse.
We have a labour inspectorate under this Minister that, with this Budget, is stretched
to breaking point trying to keep up with the breaches and the non -compliance amongst
employers in this country. It tried to do a blitz on farms. It was a random blitz on
various farms, and do you know what it found? There was 93 percent non -compliance
with the basic minimum statutory standards of emp loyment—93 percent. Then we have
a Minister who bends over backwards to encourage farming employers to pay $100 a
fortnight less than they would otherwise have to pay. No wonder the farmers think they
have got carte blanche to not comply with the basic min imum standards of our
employment law. That is the culture of employment standards in this country today. We
have a Government that cuddles up to, that licks up and down, farmers who want
nothing more than to pay their farm labourers less, and the Governmen t wonders why it
gets 93 percent non-compliance amongst the farming community.
Everything this Government has done when it comes to employment and labour
market regulation makes it harder and makes it worse for working people to get ahead
and to get a dec ent pay rise. Every law that this Government has promoted and passed
in the last 6 years has made it harder for working people to get ahead and to get a pay
rise. It started with the silly 90 -day law. One-third of employers have now signed up to
it, two-thirds cannot be bothered with it because they know it is bad law, they know it is
bad practice, and they know it is dumb, and there is no employer who can point to the
fact, as this Government claims, that they have created a job as a result of it—not a one.
Law changes like that do not create jobs; all they do is make life harder. There are
good, responsible, and sensible employers saying: “Of course we want to be able to take
people on a trial basis, but we know that to do that responsibly we should do it under the
probationary law that is still on our statute book.” We know that that law requires the
19188 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
employer—a responsible, fair, and sensible employer —to provide feedback, to treat the
worker as if they are actually a human being, and to treat them with re spect, unlike the
90-day law, which does not.
When the Government surveyed workers who had been employed under the 90 -day
law, it could not find a single one who said that they had got any feedback at all on their
so-called trial period, because what was blatantly obvious is that those workers were not
being trialled in the job. They were not being trialled; they were just being manipulated
and exploited, and kicked out the door as soon as the employer decided they no longer
wanted them or needed them. Tha t is the standard that employment law has come to in
this country.
The Minister bends over backwards to make it easy for employers to rip off their
workers. He is a Minister who does not care, frankly, about basic employment
standards. He is a Minister wh o does not care about freedom of association. He is a
Minister who does not care about freedom of choice—which workers are meant to have,
according to the international agreements we have signed up to —to belong to, or form,
a trade union. This Minister and this Government do not care.
So that is why things are getting worse for workers in this country. That is why they
are looking around, saying: “How on earth is it that this Government could get here and
be allowed to mistreat so many workers for so long?”. It is time to bring that to an end.
I want to turn briefly to health and safety because that is very important to this
country, as we all know. We have all learnt a terrible and tragic lesson with Pike River
and this Government has taken on the task to  reform and revamp our health and safety
laws. It is a pity, however, that in the spirit of this Government bending over backwards
to help employers, it could not bring itself to make WorkSafe New Zealand a tripartite
organisation. It is meant to be modell ed on the similar organisation in the UK, which is
truly tripartite, but this Government could not bring itself to do that. It was just one step
too far. So when we look at WorkSafe New Zealand, we know that it needs to be
properly supported. It will need more inspectors if it is to do its job properly, and it will
need to work pretty hard to get employers on board to deal with worker participation,
making sure that workers have a proper and fulsome say on health and safety issues in
the workplace. That is the only way they are going to get safe —working
collaboratively, cooperatively, and sensibly with their employers, even though some
employers are resistant to it. Even though some employers do not want workers to have
a real say on workplace health and saf ety, we know that the only way to reduce the
atrocious record that has built up in this country is to make sure that workers can have a
say, with impunity and without fear, and have a real say on how health and safety is
managed in their workplace and in their environs. That is absolutely essential.
If there is any shortcoming in that regard, then we will have to fix that up. The
shorter answer is this: when it comes to labour market regulation and the institutions
responsible for overseeing it, we can do better—we can do better. Unfortunately —or
perhaps fortunately; I do not know —it will not be with this Government. It will not be
with this Government if we want to improve our performance, lift wages for all New
Zealanders, and make sure that all people ge t treated fairly and properly at work so that
they can have a good, constructive relationship with their employer, based on true
collaboration and cooperation and on a genuine mutual respect, so that their choices and
the way they choose to bargain and neg otiate with their employer have to be respected
by that employer.
That is what the legal framework must deliver so that we have a good, fair system,
which fairly rewards and treats people fairly. New Zealanders expect nothing less,
neither do we, and that  is why we on this side of the Chamber will be delivering that.
New Zealanders have been waiting 6 years for it.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19189

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: What a speech of petty poi nt-
scoring from the Opposition member Andrew Little. It absolutely missed the big picture
and the great reforms that this Government has taken forward for workers and
employers alike over the last several years. Talk about the language we are hearing from
Labour people at the moment. Talk about not giving a damn or a toss. It was not as bad
as David Shearer, who swore on national radio this morning. My delicate ears could not
take the kind of language we are getting from these members. It is clearly showing  the
stress that they are under.
This Government is doing a whole lot of good in this area, and it has a very proud
record. Let us go through some of the things that we have just heard from Andrew Little
about the minimum wage —[Interruption] Well, yes. Ac tually, if we had not done that,
we would be casualising and condemning the workers he says he cares about. We were
returning things to the status quo and making sure that workers on farms got the fair go
that he says he cares about. I say “petty point -scoring” because we have seen press
releases on some really good things that this Government has done for workers, from
those members and from the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions, and it is very
disappointing, indeed, to see that kind of attitude. We have  seen a lift in the number of
labour inspectors through the Budget, so it is hard, again, to know why Andrew Little is
saying the kinds of things he is saying. We have seen minimum employment
standards—a discussion document gone out —where we are seeking to  significantly lift
things so that there are criminal penalties where there is exploitation of workers, and so
on.
What did we see from Labour and the unions? Petty point -scoring. They could not
focus on the absolute good, despite the fact, I might say, t hat the Council of Trade
Unions came into my office with the Employers and Manufacturers Association calling
for the very changes I then made. They went on Radio New Zealand National and
criticised me. Well, I say that is petty, and it would be great to se e the Labour Party
stand up for some good reforms that this Government is doing, which, if Labour was
honest with itself, it would support.
Look at the Employment Relations Amendment Bill and the changes that this
Government wants to make. It has gone thr ough the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee. There were moderate changes, and yet all we get is the scaremongering
from that side. We heard about the 90 -day trial periods. Well, what we did not hear
Andrew Little say was that a third of employers—small-business owners in this country,
which is what this country is made up of —said that they took on people whom they
would not have otherwise and they gave people a go. That is real change. That is real
difference. A third of employers gave a job to people who would not have otherwise got
one, and I say that that is pro-employers and it is pro-workers.
Frankly, it is very disappointing to see the sort of left -wing attitude we get from the
Labour Party and the Green Party —oppose, oppose, oppose, rather than be constructive
on these issues. Again, they try to find any angle on the health and safety reform to
criticise it. “Well, it is not tripartite and it is not this.” Well, it is, and I differ on that
matter from Andrew Little. But let us all agree on t his: this is the biggest health and
safety reform this country has seen in at least 20 years. There is significantly more
funding into a well -resourced regulator. There are significant law changes coming. If I
was to be cruel to the Darien Fentons and the Andrew Littles, I would say that we have
seen serious reform from this Government, when, actually, over 9 years of Labour
nothing happened—nothing happened. I think we actually need to face the facts on that
on some of these issues.
To Mr Little, I say: “ Well, if you care about workers, Mr Little, what do you say to
the 7,000 oil and gas workers in Taranaki with a party that flip -flops on issues without a
19190 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
skerrick of evidence, like the Māui’s dolphins?”. We expect to see scaremongering over
there from the Green Party on that, but to his credit, David Cunliffe finally got to the
position—the right position —that there has not been a single Māui’s dolphin harmed
from oil and gas exploration over the 40 years that that has been going on in Taranaki.
We have see n protests and we have seen calls from Labour candidates for me to be
sacked. David Cunliffe, to his credit, finally got to the right position. Well, I wonder
whether Tāmati Coffey is going to be calling for him to be sacked. We in this party care
about workers. We have done really good reforms. It is just a shame that Labour and the
Greens cannot bring themselves to support them.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Vote Labour appropriatio n. It
is kind of appropriate that I do that today, given that yesterday there was a major
celebration from The Living Wage Aotearoa New Zealand Campaign, which celebrated
the 20 businesses that have signed up to pay their workers a living wage of $18.80. I
think that is something that we should celebrate, because the only way that workers are
going to be lifted out of poverty is through decent wages and through employers
modelling the behaviour that we would like to see other employers adopt.
I note that t he Vote Labour appropriation outlines the target for the number of
interventions aimed at ensuring the minimum standards of the employment legislation
are adhered to, and the Minister of Labour referred to that. It is a crucial task, and
although he may say that the Government is reviewing the minimum standards, the fact
is that they are being breached all the time. Previous speakers have referred to this as
well. What is happening is that the labour inspectors are managing to get some
inspections done, but they are woefully underfunded. We do need more of them because
there is a lot more they could be doing. The majority of inspections that they did in the
agricultural sector, which they reported on in April, showed that most of the minimum
employment standards were not being met.
I looked at the “Fencepost Jobs” page on the Fonterra website today, which actually
is still advertising for jobs of 65 hours a week with 3 days off in 10 days. These are not
the sorts of jobs that we want people to have. We want people to have jobs where they
can actually afford to live, and where they can afford to provide for their families
without having to rely on the taxpayer to increase their ability to provide for their
families through Working for Families, which just acts  as a subsidy to employers to
keep wages low. That is what Working for Families has become. I have also seen jobs
on “Fencepost Jobs” for 55 hours a week, and when I looked at the salary that works out
to be $13.66 per hour.
This is unacceptable. This is absolutely unacceptable. The Government’s response to
this kind of thing was actually to introduce and change the regulations under the
Minimum Wage Act, which meant that workers could work long hours under the
minimum wage and have it spread out over 2 we eks. It is shocking. The Government’s
regulatory regime is shocking. What we have seen from this Government is the
exploitation of young people through the introduction of youth rates. We have seen the
introduction of less job security than ever before thr ough the introduction of the 90 -day
trials, where workers can be sacked for absolutely no reason whatsoever in their first 3
months in a job.
I remind the Committee that the bill that was set to reduce and undermine collective
bargaining and take away mini mum job security, the Employment Relations
Amendment Bill, has now stalled. That was a miserly bill. It was not a moderate
change, as was suggested by the Minister of Labour; it was an attempt to undermine
workers’ rights to the nth degree. It does not cre ate jobs, Mr Bridges, because it does
not create jobs when you force wages down. There was, of course, full employment
under slavery because the pay was so low.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19191
The fact that the Employment Relations Amendment Bill has been stalled is a great
thing. It is great that we will be able to change the Government and ditch that legislation
away from the Order Paper after September. In the meantime, it is the only thing I will
probably ever thank the Hon John Banks for.
The reason we support the living wage is bec ause we believe that workers should be
able to provide for their families and live in dignity. There are 285,000 children living
in poverty in New Zealand. Two out of five of those children have a parent who is
working. More parents than ever before are wo rking several jobs just to make ends
meet. The cost of keeping wages low, and of not lifting those 285,000 kids out of
poverty, is $6 billion to $8 billion a year. We, the taxpayers, all pay for that as well, but
it is not recorded in a budget line anywhere.
It is unreasonable that while there have been overall—
Vote agreed to.
Vote Food Safety agreed to.
Vote Immigration

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Thanks for the opportunity to take a call on Vote

items.speaker: Immigration. I ask the question
items.text: is our immigration system working well? I ask whether
the system is working well in the case of Sanil Kumar. Sanil Kumar was a young man
from Fiji who came here on a work p ermit. He was diagnosed as having end-stage renal
failure, was given dialysis, and was waiting for a kidney transplant. He was forced to
leave and go to Fiji, and he died within a very short time of returning there.
The Associate Minister of Immigration has conveniently refused to answer questions
in this House on this particular case. What she has been citing is that she did not have a
privacy waiver and therefore she could not possibly talk about this case at all. But she
knows very well that a privacy waiver does not apply to a deceased natural person. That
is excluded from the Privacy Act. In any case, if the Associate Minister and the
immigration system in New Zealand had done their work diligently they would have
reached a different decision given the  facts, as any Labour Minister of Immigration
would have done. A Labour Minister of Immigration would have reached a
compassionate decision on this particular case and this young man would be alive
today—but he is not.
So why is the system under this part icular Minister working in such a flawed way?
Let us look at the facts. The facts are that this young man, as I said, was working here,
he had end-stage kidney failure, and he started receiving dialysis. His family —two first
cousins—began the process of be ing donors, the family began raising the funds, and
they raised the $130,000 required to receive—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Dr Prasad, this is an estimates
debate on immigration. The member must tie that back  to the estimates on immigration.
It is not a debate about a medical condition or what has happened to a person. You must
tie it back to immigration.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Well, there is something happening in the funding of the
immigration sy stem that does not allow it to actually make the kinds of decisions it
should be making. The Minister is hiding behind the privacy waiver. In this particular
case, were the agencies funded well enough to provide her with the right kind of advice?
The Minis ter is hiding behind this fake notion that she wrote to me to talk about the
funding of this particular case. She says that she took the unusual step in this case of
writing to me and saying that I was making inaccurate statements.
The Minister did not wr ite to me. The Minister cannot produce any evidence.
However, the Minister did send me a copy of a letter that she had sent to David
19192 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
Cunliffe, which says that there was a $36,000 debt that Mr Sanil Kumar had for the
dialysis treatment he was receiving. So I guess the funding of health and immigration is
so bad that $36,000 is the price of a life for this particular Government. The Minister
did not write to me about that. In fact, what I did say about the funding in this particular
case was that there was no cost to the immigration system.
I knew that this family had come to a payment agreement and had said they would
pay the debt. Indeed, they started paying this debt. The uncle had taken over this debt —
a New Zealand citizen with a good job, a good family, and a good home in west
Auckland. That family would have paid this particular debt, but, indeed, the Minister
still made the decision on the basis of that. That was the first basis for the decision. Yet
the statement about there being no cost to the State was absolutely true in this particular
case.
This particular immigration decision was made based on a report that was received
by  immigration about dialysis being available in Fiji. Well, that report is also worth
considering in its detail. What is it ab out the funding of the immigration system that it
does not give this Minister enough resources to actually work out the risk that is in her
own report—a report provided to her by experts in health about an immigration decision
she has made? The report writ es very clearly about dialysis available in Fiji. It says
that—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Yes, it is about the costing, about the funding of immigration
and the decisions about this—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: We are not interested in actual procedures
in Fiji.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Well, I am trying to bring it within this particular area. I am
certainly sugges ting that the funding of immigration is not good enough. It is not
adequate to allow this Minister to make these decisions. That particular report made it
very clear that this young man risked death if he went to Fiji. Three months would be
funded. Then he would find a donor. If he did not find a donor in 3 months, he would be
taken off dialysis. It says here that he would have a few weeks to prepare for his death.
This Minister did not have the expertise, did not take the time to have a look at the
decision, and did not analyse the risks, and yet she made the decision that this young
man had to return. The decision was made on two bases. One was the amount of
resources, the funding this was going to take—that it would cost our system too much—
and the other was that dialysis was available in Fiji.
The cost was being met by the family in New Zealand, and that is a fact. They had
signed up to it. As far as dialysis in Fiji was concerned, there was no analysis of where
it was available or how he would get it, a nd yet the decision was made. So here is this
young man who went to Fiji. The last thing he said to me as he was leaving the
airport—and it is reported on television —was: “I believe this is a death sentence.” This
was a 30 -year-old man, who was in all othe r aspects fine —a kidney transplant would
have fixed him. He could have returned to Fiji and lived with his family, but this
Minister made this particular decision for reasons that are unknown. Now the Minister
is saying she does not have a privacy waiver—she is hiding behind that.
Well, a privacy waiver is on its way to the Minister. It will be available, and I want to
see what else the Minister will bring out for this particular case. The privacy waiver is
on its way. There is nothing else to be released.  This decision was made on the basis of
$36,000 worth of debt, which was being paid for, and on the basis that dialysis was
available in Fiji. All the risks were mentioned in the report, but the Minister refused to
consider that.
2 Jul 2014 Estimates Debate 19193
Where was the harm? Where  would have been the harm to New Zealand if we had
allowed this young person to stay, if our system had been generous enough to let him
stay? There is blood on the hands of those who made this decision, and they ought to
actually come out and explain, at least to the family. So far they have hidden. They have
hidden under this notion that we do not have a privacy waiver. Well, a young man need
not have died. At least we would have given him a fair crack at it with a kidney
transplant in New Zealand. Believing that there was a kidney transplant available in Fiji
or that Fijians might send him to India was such a long shot, and the Minister knew that.
It was absolutely a long shot.
Even the report produced by the Ministry of Health was a report based on a pap er
somebody gave at a conference. They did not even speak to anybody about what was
available. It was a paper somebody had given at a conference some months ago. There
are so many holes in this particular decision made by this Minister that the Minister
ought to explain. It is typical of the kinds of problems there are in the immigration
system today.
People tell me that the system is aimless. Decisions are not being made consistently
in the immigration system. Two people applying, with exactly the same ba ckground,
and even having gone to the same school, for the same kinds of job offers are receiving
very different decisions. There are many, many cases now of the immigration system
being so culturally idiotic that they will go and do interviews of families , of partners
trying to come to New Zealand —this is New Zealanders going overseas, marrying,
coming back, and their partners applying —and such a monocultural approach is being
taken to assess them that they are being denied access to New Zealand.
Decisions in the immigration system are being made by people who are driven on the
basis of numbers—the numbers of decisions they have to make. This system is broken.
This system needs fixing, and this Minister ought to take responsibility for this case and
for the system and, indeed, try to redress many of the problems that are there. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Dr Prasad
commenced his intervention on Vote Immigration in the Committee stage of the
Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill questioning whether our immigration system is
working well. Well, I can advise him and the Committee that it is working a heck of  a
lot better than it did when that member’s party was in power. When we came into office
in 2008, the immigration system was in an absolute shambles. There were thousands of
applications pending. The timeliness and quality of the decision making was poor.  The
Pacific division was in complete disarray. The Christchurch office was making its own
rules and then changing them.
I find it quite disgraceful for that member to politicise the tragedy of the Kumar
family in the way that he just did. He accuses the Associate Minister of Immigration of
hiding behind a privacy waiver. That member got a privacy waiver and then put
selective and incorrect data out into the public arena but refused —refused—to intervene
and get the Associate Minister to the position where she could tell the whole story about
that case. It is disgraceful that that member would continue to politicise that tragic
situation when he knows that under the Labour Government from 1999 to 2008 the
decision-making landscape was replete with inappropri ate decisions that unfortunately
had negative outcomes for Pacific residents with health issues. To come into this
Chamber and say that this Government has blood on its hands is an absolute disgrace. I
challenge that member to be very careful what he wishe s for, because if that privacy
waiver is ever given to the Associate Minister and the full story of that case is told, he
will be very, very embarrassed indeed and will probably be quite pleased to be leaving
this House. But I say this: the privacy waiver is a long way too late for that family. I do
19194 Estimates Debate 2 Jul 2014
not believe, even if it is now given, that it is in anybody’s interests, least of all the
Kumar family’s, to continue to litigate the facts of that case after Mr Kumar’s passing.
It is a disgrace, and that member should be ashamed.
It is not surprising that immigration policy has been very much at the forefront of the
discussions around this Budget. I am very proud of this Government’s track record on
immigration. The Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman came and spent 3 yea rs cleaning up the
mess that was left, and Nathan Guy and I have inherited a much, much sounder
Immigration New Zealand, with better timeliness, with a better quality of decision
making, and—what is very important to me —very good feedback from its clients about
the quality of that service. It is important to note that immigration is quite ubiquitous. It
extends into all areas of Government policy. I think that when one looks at the National
Government’s four priorities of responsibly managing our finances, delivering better
public services, building a more competitive economy, and rebuilding Canterbury,
immigration has an underpinning role to play in all four of those goals.
There is no doubt that we are in a global contest. We are in a contest for skills, for
foreign investment, for international students, and for tourists, and the degree to which
we succeed in that contest is very much a part of the policies, processes, and
technologies that we use to deliver a good immigration service. Under Vision 2015,
which is very much underpinned by successive Budgets, including this one, there has
been quite a transformation away from bricks and mortar and a branch -based structure.
When the service and the application processes are put online, we will see what I am
confident will be a much, much more efficient application process, where case officers
can concentrate more on the quality of the application than on chasing around after
paperwork. I think that is an important difference, and it will also achieve the
Government’s goal to have at least 70 percent of transactions with the Government
online.
But I want to move to two specific areas, and, indeed, the main one does underpin
the Government’s objective for the rebuild of Canterbury. The Minister of Labour,
Simon Bridges, and I have jointly announced over $7 million of new funding to support
the Canterbury rebuild by protecting vulnerable workers and ensuring safe workplaces
and fair workplaces. I think this is very important. I have become somewhat concerned
at th e risk that migrant exploitation, although low, could grow, particularly in the
Canterbury region as the rebuild commences. There is no doubt that we are going to
need to rely very heavily on migrant labour to assist in the rebuild. The Minister for
Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment has invested heavily in skills and training,
and we will see our young New Zealanders becoming qualified and being at the front of
the queue.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Obviously not enough, given the reliance on migrant workers.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: That is right. It is not going to be enough. We
understand that. I think both sides of the Committee accept that although there were
great opportunities for young New Zealanders —job seekers and trades trainees —to
participate in the Canterbury rebuild, given the pace and scale of the work that is
required, we are already and will in the future increasingly rely on foreign migrant
labour to assist with the rebuild. So it is important to me that  those workers understand
